He remains in prison.Pike was the first woman scheduled to be executed in the state of Tennessee in over 200 years. Her lawyers have spent decades appealing her case. In the days leading up to her scheduled execution, both the US Supreme Court and Tennessee Governor Bill Lee declined to block the execution. Since it failed, Pike's lawyers have renewed their calls for her sentence to be commuted to life in prison without the possibility of parole. Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and ShippPike lost consciousness and was taken to a local hospital following her botched execution. Her legal team believed for days that she was brain dead and expected her to be taken off life support at any moment.Pike eventually woke up and began talking again on Tuesday - her lawyer Randy Spivey said her first words were "Where am I?" and "Who are you?"At a press conference on Wednesday, her lawyers said she was shackled to the bed and suffering from pneumonia and significant swelling on her arms, while also being unable to swallow."We don't know the toll all of this will take" Spivey said of her mental health, adding that Pike felt "angry and confused".Related topicsTennesseeMore on this storyChrista Pike now walking after failed US execution, lawyer tells BBCPublished3 days agoChrista Pike has 'profound' health turnaround after botched execution, lawyers sayPublished2 days ago

title: Headmaster detained after BBC investigation into alleged sexual abuse of students
content: Image source, BBC IndonesiaImage caption, Ex-headmaster Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to students as Abah, has been accused of sexual abuseByEndang Nurdin, Rebecca Henschke, BBC Eye Investigations and BBC IndonesiaPublished10 October 2026A former headmaster of an Islamic boarding school in Indonesia has been named as a suspect in a sexual abuse investigation and detained by police, following a BBC Eye report.Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to students as Abah, led the Abul Barokat boarding school on the island of Lombok.Police reopened the case after the BBC World Service revealed accusations of sexual abuse against him, and documented how former students had gathered evidence in an effort to bring the allegations to the authorities. The story sparked public outrage and led to 12 more former students giving testimony to police.Warning: This story contains details of sexual assaultCatching My Teacher Two ex-students expose sexual abuse by teachers at Islamic boarding schools in IndonesiaWatch on iPlayerListen on SoundsOutside the UK, you can watch Catching My Teacher on YouTube, external.The student detectivesCentral to the BBC Eye investigation were former students Ziadatur Rahmah, known as Zia, and Sukma Rohana Fajar.They launched their own investigation after Zia told a former classmate, Yusron Azzahidi, that the headteacher had sexually assaulted her when she was 17. The pair had been star pupils at the school. By the time Zia confided in Yusron, she was studying in Cairo, Egypt, while he was in Jakarta. Yusron suggested they gather evidence to support Zia's allegation. Speaking to former classmates, they spoke to Sukma, who alleges that Abah attempted to rape her at the school.Yusron compiled a seven-page document detailing the allegations, and they gave it to representatives of Nahdlatul Wathan Diniyah Islamiyah (NWDI), the organisation that ran the school.Thinking the school would support them, the students say that instead, they were pressured to withdraw their accusations.In a secretly recorded phone call, Abah pleaded with Yusron to protect him and his reputation."Cover the shame of your teacher. Everyone makes mistakes, my child," Abah said.Abah also contacted Zia, who secretly recorded their conversation and shared it with the BBC. In the recording, Abah is heard apologising, but pleads with her to remain silent.Following the BBC investigation, Abah held a news conference where he denied all the allegations. He did not deny that the voice heard in the recorded calls was his, but said the recordings were not confessions.Sukma told the BBC she had been forced to sign a document saying her allegations were lies. She later secretly recorded a conversation with Abah's wife, known to students as Umi. In the recording, Umi tells Sukma that the document was intended to protect "her good name".The former students eventually resumed their efforts to seek justice, with support from lawyer Joko Jumadi, who has experience in similar cases.Figure caption, Watch: BBC tracks down abusive teacher secretly released earlyMore students come forwardThe day after the BBC investigation was published, parents arrived at the school to collect their children, with some travelling from other islands.One mother said she had begun crying when she heard the news, thinking about her daughter."I'm moving her right now," she said. "I absolutely want my child to leave this school."Yusron said he and Zia, who recently got married, were overwhelmed by the response from former students."It was beyond what we expected," he said. "So many people contacted us - on Instagram, WhatsApp. They contacted me and Zia directly, and lots of them were saying, 'I'm a victim too'."Police interviewed Zia and Sukma, along with the 12 other former students who came forward with allegations of abuse."They thought they were the only ones - and it's been really shocking for them to learn, like I did, that they weren't alone," Zia said.Sukma said she felt relieved and grateful that the allegations are now being taken seriously."It's not about revenge. It's more the acknowledgement that what he did was wrong. I'm waiting for the day when he admits that himself," she told the BBC.Abah has resigned from the school and has said he will respect the legal process.The BBC contacted Abah and his wife during its original investigation, but they did not respond at the time.NWDI denied trying to cover up the allegations and said it was investigating them internally. It said it had a duty to protect the organisation from being tarnished by the alleged actions of individuals.In the wake of the BBC investigation, NWDI vowed to ensure such abuse never happened again and said it would safeguard the rights of students who came forward.Related topicsIndonesiaSexual violenceAsia

title: Woman injures three people in third Poland school knife attack in a week
content: Image source, Agencja Wyborcza.pl via ReutersByRorey BosottiPublished10 October 2026A woman has been arrested after injuring three people in a third knife attack recorded at schools in Poland this week.The 21-year-old used a "dangerous object" to attack a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in the capital, Warsaw, police told news agencies PAP and AP.It comes a day after thousands of police visited schools across Poland, following two stabbing attacks earlier in the week, one of which led to the killing of a female caretaker.A Warsaw police spokesperson said they could not confirm whether the latest incident was related to the two previous attacks.Authorities told local media that the 17-year-old injured on Saturday had been taken to hospital, but her condition was not life-threatening. Two other women aged 17 and 24, who had gone in to submit enrolment documents, were also injured, Poland's state news agency reported.Police told local media that the suspected attacker was a student at the school and initial findings suggested that she did not know the three victims.Schools in Poland had been stepping up security following knife attacks at schools across the country on 7 and 8 October. Polish police said they had detained 76 people after deploying to schools across the country."When it comes to the safety of Polish children and peace in our schools, there is no room for compromise," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said ahead of the operation.Local media, citing a police spokesperson, reported authorities had information to suggest incidents this past week could be related to an internet challenge.On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student attacked and injured nine people at a vocational school in the central Polish province of Mazovian.A day later, a 37-year-old caretaker was killed after a 15-year-old entered a primary school in Leszczydół-Nowiny, north of Warsaw.Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński also said a 17-year-old was detained in the town of Sierpc, north-west of Warsaw, after allegedly stating "on school grounds that he planned to do something... dangerous - that he intended to harm someone".Related topicsPolandKnife crime

title: Nobel peace laureate says US sanctions on ICC 'unacceptable'
content: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The South African former ICC judge was awarded the prize on FridayByGeorge WrightPublished10 October 2026Navi Pillay, the winner of this year's Nobel Peace Prize, has called US sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) "unheard of" and "unacceptable".The South African former ICC judge was awarded the prize on Friday "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.US President Donald Trump expressed his disatisfaction with the pick and hours later the US unveiled sweeping sanctions in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it described as a "rogue" institution.The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.Pillay, speaking via video link during an event at the Nobel Peace Center in Oslo on Saturday, said: "There is so much tension and anxiety over the continued existence of international courts, mainly the International Criminal Court in The Hague."Most importantly, sanctions have been announced by one country against the judges, just for the judicial orders they issue. This is unheard of, unacceptable." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier said the sanctions - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.The US has already sanctioned 17 ICC judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to inhibit its ability to operate financially.However, the US has provided a six-month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns.The Trump administration claims that the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty.It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted.UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar".The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in saying they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions.Figure caption, Watch: Who is Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay?Pillay, 85, also served as UN rights chief, taking part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza.Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country's fifth Peace Prize winner - following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu."If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked after receiving the prize, a reference to last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition figure María Corina Machado, deciding to gift her prize to the US president.Trump called the announcement of Pillay as 2026's winner "disgraceful and embarassing", and an "indelible stain on the country of Norway". He has long indicated he thought he should have been awarded the prestigious prize, and was nominated by several allies for it last year.Related topicsInternational Criminal CourtDonald TrumpUnited StatesNobel PrizeHuman rightsMore on this storyUS unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'Published2 days ago'Stain on the country': Trump criticises Norway over Nobel Peace PrizePublished1 day ago

title: Riyadh airport attacks another dangerous moment in already tense conflict
content: Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, Houthi soldiers stand guard during a protest against Saudi Arabia, in Sana'a, Yemen, on FridayByFrank Gardner, BBC security correspondent and Jon Donnison, Reporting fromJerusalemPublished11 October 2026, 12:32 BSTUpdated 7 hours agoThe attacks on King Khalid Airport in Riyadh mark another dangerous moment in a region that is already fraught with tension and conflict.Saudi Arabia wasn't ready for this. In recent weeks the Houthis have stepped up their attacks on Saudi Arabian soil, but their attacks over the past few days have hit the country's critical infrastructure in the form of the capital's main airport, apparently penetrating Saudi air defences with ease.Saturday's attack killed 12 people and hurt more than 300. On Sunday the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said an "unknown projectile" had hit a passenger hall and a cruise missile had been intercepted nearby.The physical damage can be quickly repaired, but the country's reputation as a safe haven of stability is taking a battering.As well as all the airport attacks, the Houthis have sought to take control of strategically significant positions along the Red Sea coast and around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. This further increases the risk to safe navigation along the vital maritime corridor - although the Yemeni government says it has "secured" the strait.The civil war in Yemen between the country's government - which is internationally recognised and supported by Saudi Arabia - and the Houthis, who are backed by Iran, has been going on for more than a decade. It has left many thousands of people dead and plunged Yemen into one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.It is a complex and often confusing geopolitical conflict, and this latest escalation needs to be seen in the broader context of the tension between Iran, the United States and Israel.Who are the Houthis and what do they want?Published24 SeptemberHouthi attacks raise fears of wider Middle East conflict and more global economic damagePublished24 JulyChildren brave snipers and mortars to go to school near Yemen front line Published5 days agoNot since the al-Qaeda insurgency of the mid-2000s has the Kingdom faced such a serious threat. The Saudi government overcame that challenge through an effective hearts and minds campaign. Then it weathered the Arab Spring uprisings around the region which saw off leaders in Tunisia, Libya, Egypt and Yemen. It even shrugged off – with some annoyance – an Iranian ballistic missile attack on Riyadh in March.But this is different. Saudi Arabia may have one of the most powerful air forces in the Middle East, and it has been carrying out devastating air strikes on Houthi positions. Despite this, the opposing forces have managed to seize large portions of the country, particularly in the north and west.But the Houthis know exactly where to hit back: at the soft underbelly of the Saudi economy.As part of the "axis of resistance", the Houthis are a vital strategic partner for Iran. From Jizan on the Red Sea to the petrochemical complex at Khurais, the Houthis are delivering explosive drones and missiles with deadly accuracy.The Red Sea shipping route has become increasingly important, because the Strait of Hormuz, on the other side of the Gulf, has still not fully reopened since the US and Iran have failed to reach a deal to end their war.Targeting ships in the Red Sea is another way that the Houthis are trying to exert leverage - the attacks cause global economic damage, which is a key bargaining chip for Tehran.In early September, the White House stated it would not directly intervene in the Yemen conflict, but could provide intelligence support to the Saudis. It later confirmed that it was supplying intelligence and had deployed military experts to Saudi Arabia.However the situation may have taken a new turn following the latest attack on Riyadh, which killed a US citizen.Speaking to reporters, US President Donald Trump called Saturday's attack "terrible" and indicated he may intervene militarily with the Saudis. "We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," Trump said.But that now seems unlikely, at least before crucial US midterm elections next month.When he was re-elected in 2024, Trump promised to end America's role in wars around the world. Despite this, the US is currently involved in three unresolved conflicts in the Middle East - in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.Should Trump get embroiled in another one, this time in Yemen, it is unlikely to go down well with voters.This war now looks like it will intensify before it ends in another shaky truce - with or without US involvement.Additional analysis from Abdelbassir Hassan, BBC ArabicRelated topicsHouthis IranYemenSaudi ArabiaYemen crisisUnited StatesMore on this storySaudi Arabia's Riyadh airport hit by second Houthi strike in two daysPublished30 minutes agoInside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for controlPublished27 SeptemberYemen's government announces all-out war to reclaim land from HouthisPublished4 October

title: Blackpink’s Lisa Manobal: How the K-pop star faced a race scandal
content: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lisa, who was born Pranpriya Manobal in Thailand, became one of the world's most-recognisable K-pop idols as a member of BlackpinkByMark SavageMusic correspondentPublished11 October 2026, 00:31 BSTWhat's it like to be the main character of an online scandal?That's one of the questions raised in a new documentary about Lisa Manobal – one quarter of K-pop phenomenon Blackpink and a breakout star of TV show The White Lotus.The film captures an unfolding controversy, as leaked videos show Blackpink using racial slurs when they were teenage trainees in the K-pop system.The clips, which emerged last year, showed the band covering US rap songs during rehearsals. Explicit language, including the n-word, was left uncensored. The scandal blew up while Lisa was rehearsing for a pivotal performance at the Coachella Festival in 2025.Offended and upset, some fans demanded an apology - but the band's record label, forbade the members from issuing a statement.With Lisa's team in crisis mode, documentarian Sue Kim followed Lisa into her dressing room."I said, 'Look, I know this is new. I know you guys are wildly confused and hurt, but this is your time to say whatever you want to say - even if you're just processing your thoughts and telling us what you're feeling," Kim tells the BBC.The film-maker "honestly expected her to say no".Instead, Lisa lay down on a sofa and spoke from the heart."It's bad," the singer says in the documentary, with a mixture of shame and nerves.Lisa explains she was "15 or 16" when the videos were shot and "didn't know that [word] was sensitive because I'm from Thailand and my first language is not English".Having only heard the term in rap music, she was unaware of its offensive history."Now I would never ever do that because, now, I've got education," she says. "Now I know better."But I did wrong."It is a vulnerable and human response - and nothing like the scripted PR apology you might expect. (Lisa has since apologised publicly, external in an interview with Variety, although some people remained unconvinced, external).Kim says Lisa’s in-the-moment reaction is "one of the most important scenes" in her documentary, Always Lalisa, which hits cinemas on Monday, 12 October."There was no premeditation on Lisa's part, there was no media training," she adds."I asked her one question and she just talked for an hour, and everything came out, and it's all stream of consciousness."And what you see with Lisa in that moment is so genuine, it's impossible not to feel compassion for her."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Sue Kim (right) followed Lisa for a year, as she launched her solo career during a break in Blackpink's activitiesThe incident overshadowed what was supposed to be a triumphant launch for Lisa's debut solo album, Alter Ego.In the film, the singer receives death threats, but presses ahead with public appearances while safety concerns are "spinning in my head"."To a certain extent I have to take [criticism] and compromise," she says, exhausted, "but sometimes, it's too much".In a world of sanitised celebrity profiles, Kim's portrayal of upheaval and discomfort is unusual. She asks Lisa about bad reviews, and captures the star being scolded by her vocal coach for lack of effort.That said, the documentary was commissioned by the film division of the star's record label (which also made the recent, and much less revealing, Oasis documentary), so it is still ultimately a marketing product.Even the most abrasive moments are calibrated to present Lisa in a good light - but the director credits the star with ensuring the film was not a mere puff piece."You never know when you meet an artist how transparent they'll be. And I have to give all credit to Lisa because she allowed us almost total access," Kim says."And when I showed her the film, she never asked me to remove a single scene. That's exceptional."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lisa put aside scandal and online death threats to put on one of the standout performances of 2025's Coachella Music FestivalImage source, Sony Music VisionImage caption, The documentary captures Lisa's joy - and relief - after she pulled off the hour-long showThe film's main storyline is about Lisa taking a break from K-pop to pursue crossover success in the Western music market.When we meet her, she is one of the world's most famous women, with millions of record sales and brand deals with Louis Vuitton and Bvlgari.But she is trapped by a K-pop system that forbids her from drinking alcohol and having adult relationships."I don't want my dating to be the thing to hurt Blackpink's popularity," she says in the film. "But when I turned 25, I realised that this is not how you're supposed to live your life."As a result, Lisa makes an early decision to cut ties with Korean entertainment company YG, who discovered her as a teenager, and signs a new deal with RCA Records in the US."Knowing her as I do, that took an immense amount of courage," says Kim."In general, she is a very kind, sweet person - and sometimes personalities like that, they don't want to rock the boat."Having been trained in the K-pop system from an early age, she grew acclimatised to obedience. Declaring that she wants a break is such a disruption to that way of life that I can only imagine it must have been building inside her for years."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Blackpink are one of K-pop's biggest bands, with hits like Whistle, How You Like That and Kill This LoveThe potential rewards for going solo were phenomenal – but so were the risks.In the film, we see Lisa struggling to assert herself in the recording studio, and tearfully battling nerves over her singing voice.At the age of 25, she is still curiously child-like. The fierce independence of her solo single New Woman sounds more like aspiration than fact.Kim says that began to change as they filmed."I saw a person who was very tentative and unsure of herself slowly starting to unfold her wings. Making mistakes, but also getting back up on the horse."Kim locates an inner confidence in early home videos of Lisa competing in talent shows, drawing parallels between that precocious seven-year-old and the young woman who is gradually reclaiming her agency.She doggedly pursues a role in the third season of hit TV drama The White Lotus, self-taping an audition that wins her the role of kind-hearted wellness coach Mook Sornsin.On set, she shrugs off the restrictive moral code of her pop career."Lisa threw more parties than anyone else," notes the show's executive producer in an interview."And the defining characteristic of a Lisa party is tequila shots."Image source, Fabio Lovino / HBOImage caption, The singer made her acting debut in season three of The White Lotus, filmed on location in her home countryKim did not partake in the hedonism. In fact, the film-maker and her crew were regularly falling sick as they tried to keep up with Lisa's ridiculous schedule."But when we premiered the film in Toronto, Lisa found me and she brought bottles of tequila, and that was like the perfect christening of the film," she laughs.The movie ends in June 2025 as Lisa returns to Seoul and rejoins Blackpink. As she unpacks her bags, she is clearly conflicted."It's bittersweet, and I think that's OK," says Kim."I don't think people should take it as like, 'Oh, she hates Blackpink'. It's more that she was reflecting on this year of freedom and worrying that she wouldn't be able to retain that. And that's a very astute fear to have."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lisa won the award for best pop act at this year's MTV Awards, becoming the first K-pop star to lift the trophyIn the year since, Lisa has already wrapped up her Blackpink duties and started phase two of her solo career with the single Sawadika. Kim says she is not surprised."Spending the year away from the K-pop system in the US really opened her horizons," the director says."She was exposed to a different kind of entertainment system where they're not held to a vow of chastity. If two star performers link up, it's almost like they get more power."That gave her a sense of like, 'Oh, I could have a different life. I might not lose my career if I want to get married and have children'."So I think part of the reason why Lisa's interested in continuing her solo career is that it might give her a little bit more personal freedom to be who she is."Related topicsFilmK-popBLACKPINKMusicMore on this storyBlackpink: K-pop band make 'epic Wembley dream' come truePublished16 August 2025From Squid Game to Blackpink, how South Korea became a culture powerhousePublished28 December 2024Blackpink star Lisa joins White Lotus castPublished13 February 2024

title: Myanmar's young men live in fear of being snatched off the streets and sold to the army
content: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Authorities in Myanmar have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas, leading to corruption, extortion and abductionsByGavin Butler and BBC Burmese Published10 October 2026You do not stay out after dark if you're young and able-bodied in Hpa-An, the capital of Myanmar's southern Karen state. In recent months this has become conventional wisdom.But Zaw Min has no choice."I worry, but I have to go out to work," says the 26-year-old tuk tuk driver, who asked that his real name be omitted out of fear for his safety. "My family call me all the time and remind me not to drive passengers too far; to be careful who I take as a passenger... I have to be vigilant all the time."People are panicked and frightened," he explains. "Some people I know have been taken."Locals say plain-clothed members and supporters of the Myanmar junta have been roaming the streets of Hpa-An, arbitrarily arresting people in their teens, 20s and 30s and forcing them into military service.According to leaked documents seen by BBC Burmese, authorities have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas across jurisdictions, bolstering the junta's ranks as it endures a war of attrition against ethnic militias, pro-democracy groups and civilian-led resistance movements.Zaw Min is the only one among his siblings who is at the age of recruitment. Many other "kids" his age have fled, he says – to Thailand, or the homes of relatives further afield. Those who remain are often under strict instructions from their parents: be home before dusk.Myanmar has been locked in a bloody civil war since February 2021, when its own military launched a coup d'etat and ousted democratically elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi.Three years later, following a string of humiliating losses, plummeting morale and soaring rates of desertion, the junta enacted a mandatory conscription law that required all men aged 18 to 35 and women aged 18 to 27 to serve at least two years under military command. Those who refuse face up to five years in prison.The enactment of the law "represents one of the most severe and impactful actions taken against the entire civilian population since the military coup", according to Maj Naung Yoe, military affairs official at the Myanmar Defense and Security Institute (MDSI) and a former military officer who defected and joined the anti-coup Civil Disobedience Movement.Image source, Telegram/@pyithusittImage caption, An estimated 100,000 young recruits have been conscripted by the junta since early 2024Hpa-An is the latest to be caught in a dragnet that's already ensnared an estimated 100,000 young recruits over the past two-and-a-half years – many of them via coercion, extortion and abductions."Security forces track young people's movements to arrest them, force them into service under the pretext of statutory military eligibility, extort money through threats of detention, and arrest individuals during guest-list inspections," Naung Yoe says.The BBC contacted the Myanmar government's Central Body for Summoning People's Military Servants regarding incidents mentioned in this story, including the forced recruitment of conscripts and reports of abductions allegedly carried out in recent months.They said they had no comment on the matter.With the mandatory conscription law, the junta has established a human supply chain to sustain its armed forces. And it appears to have worked. Observers note that reinforcements have played a critical role in helping the regime claw back more territory. In many parts of Myanmar, the resistance is now on the back foot.The war, though, is far from over. And as more youths evade conscription – either to join the resistance or simply avoid armed conflict against their fellow countrymen – the junta's recruitment methods have become ever more extreme.International rights groups such as Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and Fortify Rights say Myanmar's military is abducting civilians and forcing them into military service.In July, open-source research organisation Myanmar Witness revealed that they had analysed hundreds of missing-person advertisements collected from Facebook between 2021 and 2025. Researchers found that missing person notices for January rose from four in 2021, pre-coup, to 82 in 2025, post-conscription law. "In practice, much of [the Myanmar military's] recruitment appears to be carried out through detention, coercion, and disappearance rather than formal call-up, and often without notice to families," they concluded.Men and boys constituted the majority of reported missing persons.Figure caption, Watch: BBC goes into jungle with Myanmar's civil war rebels"They are spreading rumours all over the neighbourhood that I sold my husband."Ma Moe San Pan sobs the words through gulps of air. She is sitting in her kitchen, at home in Yangon, where on the morning of 8 May 2025 she saw her 33-year-old husband Phyo Wai for the last time."We had an argument, and afterwards he left home," she recalls."I was upset and told my cousin about what had happened."Ma Moe San Pan's cousin worked at the local ward administration office, and she asked him to bring her husband back. It was two days later that Phyo Wai called her, from a military recruitment centre on the other side of the city.The cousin had taken him to the ward office which had sold him on to another ward for 4 million kyats ($900; £680) to fill that ward's recruitment quota, Ma Moe San Pan says. The BBC was unable to reach Ma Moe San Pan's cousin.In a desperate attempt to bring him back, Ma Moe San Pan was then scammed out of 4.5 million kyats by strangers who falsely promised his release.U Maung Maung Lwin, the administrator of the ward to which Phyo Wai was taken, later admitted to the BBC that he had played a role in sending him to the military recruitment authorities. When asked about allegations that individuals were being conscripted outside their home township, he said transfers from other townships do occur when local quotas cannot be met.But he denied that any money was involved in such cases, or in Phyo Wai's forced conscription."[Phyo Wai] told me they said they would help him and made him sign documents," Ma Moe San Pan recalls."If my husband had been legally selected for conscription through the normal process, I could have accepted that. What I cannot accept is that our own ward administration office allegedly sold him to another ward."I also regret placing my trust in my cousin."Image source, BBC BurmeseImage caption, Ma Moe San Pan says her husband was sold into military service by her own cousinIn the time since Phyo Wai was taken, Ma Moe San Pan has filed police complaints relating to two matters: the sale of her husband into military service, and the 4.5 million kyats she lost to scammers.The police accepted her complaint, she says, but refused her request to include human trafficking charges, claiming a human trafficking case could only be registered if a person had been sold abroad.She does not know where her husband is now.Ma Moe San Pan's case highlights a grim mutation of the junta's mandatory conscription laws: mounting pressure from the higher levels of the regime has created perverse incentives further down the chain of command.Surging demand and dwindling supply have fuelled an illicit market for eligible recruits. And with money on the table, security officials have taken to arresting youth at road checkpoints, tracking and ambushing workers during their daily commutes, setting traps via fake job advertisements, and forcibly entering people's homes, Naung Yoe says."Under the guise of the conscription law, these coercive arrests and recruitment drives have effectively transformed into a modern-day slavery and human trafficking enterprise."In late August, police in Yangon arrested a member of the Fire Services Department – a branch of the home affairs ministry – and his son-in-law for abducting four young men with the intention of selling them for military conscription.The reserve fire brigade unit commander allegedly deceived the men with promises of employment opportunities, luring them to his house and trapping them in a series of purpose-built detention rooms. Police officers raided the residence and arrested him on 25 August. He has since been charged with kidnapping or abducting in order to wrongfully confine a person, and faces up to 7 years in prison. BBC Burmese made several attempts to contact the police station where he is being held, but was unsuccessful."Lower-level administrative bodies, military personnel and local criminal gangs employ diverse tactics to press-gang and arrest young people," Naung Yoe says. "They sell these individuals to military units and regional commands facing manpower shortages, or traffic substitute recruits on behalf of wealthier individuals seeking to buy their way out of service."Image source, BBC BurmeseImage caption, It's been more than a year since Ma Moe San Pan last saw her husband Phyo WaiWhile conscription orders are indiscriminate on paper – demanding a quota of recruits from each village, ward, or township proportional to its population – wealthier conscripts can simply pay to dodge the draft and be replaced by someone more financially vulnerable.So it is the poor who disproportionately bear the burden.Naung Yoe, meanwhile, told the BBC that "these practices are escalating due to increasing difficulties in meeting monthly recruitment quotas and the lucrative financial profits made from recruit trading at the ground level".But the hardening fist of forced conscription also reveals the junta's empty hand, and its desperation for manpower.It "seems to be another step in the junta's efforts to enlist unwilling youth in a conflict that underscores its embattled position in the civil war" says Dr Sandeep Singh, a research fellow who teaches military studies at the National University of Singapore.The climate surrounding routine abductions, he adds, has "generated further difficulties on the youth of Myanmar, already affected by years of civil war, and their families".In addition to the daily anxiety of life in Myanmar, many would-be recruits now fear being forced to fight in a deadly conflict that they not only don't believe in, but actively oppose. This constant threat has fuelled massive internal displacement and severe labour shortages in an already flailing economy, and sent people fleeing to neighbouring countries.Having spent more than half a decade waging war against its own population, the junta is now wielding the conscription law as yet another tool of subjugation, observers say.As the MDSI put it in a statement published in June: "The generals have benefited by using military law to make the citizens fight against each other."Related topicsMyanmarAsiaMilitaryMore on this storyMillions opposed military rule in Myanmar. Is their dream of a revolution over?Published30 JulyFrom behind bars, Aung San Suu Kyi casts a long shadow over MyanmarPublished14 JanuarySoldier-spies in Myanmar help pro-democracy rebels make crucial gainsPublished20 December 2024The college scam that promised students fleeing war a new life in FinlandPublished12 June

title: Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago - why are they resuming now?
content: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, An estimated crowd of 20,000 gathered in Kentucky in 1936 for the public hanging of Rainey BetheaBySheila FlynnSenior US reporterPublished10 October 2026They came in their thousands from near and far. Men, women and children lined up on a Kentucky riverfront for the public hanging of a black man convicted of raping and killing an elderly white widow.It was 14 August 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky, a sweltering Friday in the middle of a legendary heatwave. Some slept overnight near the gallows to preserve their spots. Others held "necktie" parties the previous evening, arriving hungover as teenagers sold popcorn and soda to spectators.By the execution time of 05:00, the crowd had swelled to an estimated 20,000.That's when Rainey Bethea, an orphan in his 20s, stepped up to the gallows - sentenced to death after allegedly confessing to robbing, raping and killing Lischia Edwards, 70.The previous afternoon, he'd eaten a last meal of fried chicken, pork chops, mashed potatoes, pickled cucumbers, cornbread, lemon pie and ice cream.Many of those gathered - including press from as far away as Chicago and New York - came to see the rumoured "Lady Executioner". The local sheriff had died four months earlier and his widow had become his unlikely replacement. She declined to pull the trip lever herself, however, and it was a hired hangmen who instead sent Bethea to his death.That moment marked the last high-profile public hanging in the US. The circus surrounding Bethea's death embarrassed many in Kentucky and the governor outlawed public executions 18 months later.By then, most states had abolished capital punishment in view of the masses as societal attitudes sought more humane and private methods. Another hanging was attended by a few hundred in Missouri in 1937, but that was lesser known and marked America's final public execution - until now.Image source, FPG/Staff/GettyImage caption, Men, women and children attended the hanging, which marked the last high-profile public execution in the USA little more than 90 years after Bethea's killing, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the military would publicly execute Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 unarmed fellow soldiers in 2009 at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.The Pentagon followed up by saying the execution by firing squad in December would be livestreamed."People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.University of Colorado professor emeritus Michael Radelet, a long-time scholar of capital punishment, was shocked."I never imagined [another] public execution," he told the BBC.He noted how public support for the death penalty in general has been steadily declining - it was at 80% in 1994, for example, but now stands at 52%."It's gone down precipitously, especially when you give the alternative of life without parole," he said.It's too soon to know what the American public thinks of the idea of livestreaming an execution. But it's likely that millions or more will tune in.With Hegseth's announcement, Radelet said, "the justification for the death penalty becomes entertainment... bring your popcorn, invite your friends". Figure caption, Americans discuss their views on the death penalty after the botched execution in Tennessee of convicted murderer Christa PikeSonya Lea, who just last year published a book about Bethea's execution, "felt absolute horror for our descendants" when she heard of the announced firing squad livestream."What they called it in 1936 was a carnival of sadism," she said. "That we now have the technology that can make it go wider than the 20,000 people who showed up... to witness in Owensboro, Kentucky, it just makes it even more horrific."Lea's grandparents were teenage newlyweds among that 1936 crowd. She only found out after her grandmother's death in 2002, when she read an account her late grandma had given detailing how they were close enough to hear Bethea's neck snap.The author's subsequent years of research taught her that many Kentuckians were "haunted" by that execution."I really thought, with all my heart, that we had put this in the rearview mirror, this level of grotesquery that only a few countries in the world engage in - Iran, North Korea, Afghanistan," she said. "Are we now, as the United States of America, considering ourselves to be part of that kind of government? It's just horrific."But the polarisation and rhetoric in US politics may have set the stage for such an announcement, said Kurt Gray, a social psychology professor at Ohio State University."Some Americans might thirst for blood, but I think a lot of Americans don't and, if anything, I think a lot of other Americans are just kind of maybe desensitised," he said. "So it's not like they're cheering a public execution - they're just like, 'Oh, yeah, I guess that's where we're at now.'"Figure caption, Can the Fort Hood shooter’s execution be livestreamed?Other research indicates that Hegseth and the administration may be reading the country wrong.Garen Wintemute, director of the Violence Prevention Research Program at the University of California, Berkeley, said surveys point to a declining appetite for violence in the US."This morning, the chair of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops labelled this [livestream execution announcement] as barbaric," he said. "And I think he speaks for a lot of people.""I think it's this: a public execution is not who we are," he added. "It's not who we aspire to be as a country."The debate over Hegseth's surprise announcement appeared to be playing out within the White House on Friday. US Vice-President JD Vance expressed uncertainty to reporters about whether the public execution would go ahead as planned and said he would not watch it if it were livestreamed.Hours later, US President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan but that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.He did not answer the question of whether he'd watch Hasan's execution. "I really don't care how he goes as long as he goes," Trump said. "And I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."Related topicsUnited StatesKentuckyMore on this storyWho is Nidal Hasan? What to know about US plans to livestream an execution onlinePublished1 day agoFort Hood survivor supports gunman's execution by firing squad but questions livestreamPublished2 days agoI've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike'sPublished2 October

title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
content: Image source, Swedish Coast GuardImage caption, Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022BySarah RainsfordEastern and Southern Europe correspondentPublished10 October 2026Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children.Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks.But German police were already closing in on him.After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany.Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine".Both he and his country have denied any involvement.Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Police escort Serhii K to a helicopter following a hearing with the German Federal Public Prosecutor It was 02:03 on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea.There were two further explosions targeting both Nord Stream 2 – not yet in action, but already full – and the original Nord Stream 1 that had supplied around half of Germany's annual demand for natural gas.Both have been inoperable ever since.Prosecutors say "high-performance explosives" were planted approximately 80m (260ft) below the surface: four devices weighing up to 27kg each, activated with timers.They "strongly suspect" that Serhii K led a crew that included four deep-sea divers, using a rented yacht called Andromeda.Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat.As word of the blasts spread, experts and some governments initially rushed to the same conclusion: they blamed Moscow.Russia had a history of hybrid attacks, after all, and of using its energy supplies for political pressure.But as the airwaves filled with commentators citing "suspicious" Russian naval activity near the blast site, German police ignored the noise.They went on following the forensic crumbs.Eventually they led to Ukraine.The case since built by investigators alleges that Serhii K entered Germany for the Nord Stream attack on a forged passport, likely issued by Ukraine's security services.In the extradition files sent to Italy he is named as Serhii Kulinich.That might explain why he looked so calm on his holiday in Italy.He had been travelling widely, and without incident, for the past year. In a copy of his real passport seen by the BBC there are more than two dozen stamps from countries including France, Spain and Canada – all dated after the Nord Stream attacks.But by 13 August 2025, Germany had identified its key suspect and this time, when Serhii K crossed into Poland, he was detected.Italian police say the actual arrest warrant was only issued on 18 August after he had travelled south and left Poland, suggesting the Germans were not sure their neighbours would co-operate and detain him.By the time his wife made a booking at La Pescaccia though, he was officially a "wanted" man. As soon as he showed his passport at check-in at the resort, the local carabinieri got an automatic alert.Police arrived to make their arrest late that night, leading Serhii K away from the glamping site and his family in handcuffs.The saboteursNone of the Nord Stream suspects have spoken publicly and no-one admits any role in the explosions.But I have talked to some of the Ukrainians caught up in the case, and people close to them."Anyone who admits involvement in this mission, they're immediately a target for Russia," one source explained. "Whoever did it can never confirm that."Nord Stream was a major investment and worth big money to Moscow in fuel sales. But it also made Germany and others dependent, giving Russia immense leverage over Europe.That is why Ukraine, the US and Poland in particular all loathed it.Another source I spoke to was "eaten alive by anxiety" over the investigation and baffled that Germany, a close ally of Ukraine, was even pursuing prosecution."Many Ukrainians believe that these pipelines, they helped Russia to fight so blowing them up was a good thing for our country," they pointed out.The German prosecutor's office told me the justice system was outside of any politics. Sabotage is an offence against Germany's constitution.Equally frustrating for the Ukrainians I met was their own government's silence."At the very minimum, he's a military man, so if there are any questions, they should be addressed to the state, not to him," a close contact of Serhii K complained.Ahead of his extradition to Germany, his lawyer here in Italy told me his client had felt "abandoned".Image source, Omar Marques/Getty ImagesImage caption, Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from CroatiaGermany has a whole list of suspects, but only one other name has been revealed so far.Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August.He was there as a consultant on a new thriller film about the Nord Stream blasts, though he denies any role in the real-life operation.Travelling was a risky move, when he knew Germany was pursuing him.Zhuravylov has lived in Warsaw with his family since just before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and has his own business there installing air conditioning.He is also a keen and competent deep-sea diver.But he is a civilian.Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him.In a dramatic twist, he ruled instead that a Ukrainian attack on Nord Stream, if that was what happened, would be a "just" act in a "bloody and genocidal war".As one source close to the case put it to me: "The Poles don't like Ukrainians, historically, but they hate Russians and Germans even more."Croatia is a different matter.Political ripplesThe implications of this case reach far beyond the courthouse in Hamburg.After a slow start, Germany is now Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid. The far-right AfD party, currently riding high in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream case to bolster its argument that support for Kyiv needs to stop.It is awkward, at the very least, for the governments in both Berlin and Kyiv.It also raises questions about what constitutes a legitimate military target: who can hit what, and where, outside an open war zone.When asked about the explosions, President Zelensky has previously insisted that Ukraine "definitely didn't do that".This week, a foreign ministry spokesman went further."I find it very unfortunate that this entire discussion has come to focus on who blew [the pipelines] up, rather than who built them," Heorhii Tykhyi told the BBC, forcefully.He argued that Nord Stream had "untied Russia's hands" to go to war, because it no longer needed to transit Ukraine for its gas to reach Europe. "Did we warn about this? We did," Tykhyi wanted to know. "Did anyone listen to us? No, no-one did."First in the dockSerhii K will shortly become the first suspect to face charges in this high profile trial.Zhuravlyov's case could be merged, in theory, at a later date, though that would be complicated.Those who know Serhii K call him a patriot.He signed up to defend Ukraine when Russia invaded even though he had several children and was exempt - and fought until December 2023.His military ID shows that he was still in active service when the pipelines were blown up, meaning someone in Ukraine's military command knew exactly where he was and what he was doing.They are not saying, though.And in court Serhii K himself will not say a word, either.His legal team will argue that he is not authorised to reveal details of any activities as a soldier and produce sworn statements from two of his military superiors to back that up.I am told one of them will be the man widely named as the mastermind of the entire Nord Stream plot.Related topicsUkraineGermanyWar in UkraineMore on the Nord Stream blastsUkrainian man arrested in Croatia over Nord Stream pipeline blastsPublished19 AugustSabotage behind Nord Stream gas leaks, says EUPublished28 September 2022A journey to the site of the Nord Stream explosionsPublished18 November 2022

title: Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?
content: Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?CloseUS President Donald Trump has said Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an immediate "energy ceasefire".Moscow is yet to comment on the announcement and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky told US media it was "news to me".Trump also recently announced a US deal to import Russian diesel, in an attempt to bring the fuel price down ahead of the midterm elections.The price of diesel in the US has been high since the start of the war with Iran and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz.The BBC's Joe Inwood examines Trump's announcement and what might mean for the president ahead of the midterm election.More on this story.SubsectionWorldPublished2 hours agoShareclose panelShare pageCopy linkAbout sharingRelated topicsDonald TrumpFollow Donald Trumpclose panelYou are now following Donald TrumpUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.Volodymyr ZelenskyFollow Volodymyr Zelenskyclose panelYou are now following Volodymyr ZelenskyUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.Vladimir PutinFollow Vladimir Putinclose panelYou are now following Vladimir PutinUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.War in UkraineFollow War in Ukraineclose panelYou are now following War in UkraineUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.Read description

title: Buildings swept away as flash floods hit central Nepal
content: Buildings swept away as flash floods hit central NepalBuildings swept away as flash floods hit central NepalCloseA flash flood has washed away houses, bridges and damaged a hydropower project along a river in central Nepal. The army said on Sunday that it had rescued 49 people from flood affected areas, but five are still missing, the district's top official confirmed. It is believed that the flood was caused by a landslide upstream of the Budhi Gandaki River in the Gorkha district. Four bridges and nearly two dozen houses have been swept away, as well as a camp at a hydropower project along the river. Nepal is still trying to recover from catastrophic floods and landslides that swept through its border towns with Tibet two months ago, wiping out thousands of houses, destroying critical energy infrastructure and leaving thousands dead and missing.More on this story.SubsectionAsiaPublished12 hours agoShareclose panelShare pageCopy linkAbout sharingRelated topicsNepalFollow Nepalclose panelYou are now following NepalUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.FloodsFollow Floodsclose panelYou are now following FloodsUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.Read description

title: Why have hundreds of 'cockroach' protesters been detained in Delhi
content: Why have hundreds of 'cockroach' protesters been detained in DelhiWhy have hundreds of 'cockroach' protesters been detained in DelhiCloseProtesters were heard slamming on bus windows following their detention during an anti-government demonstration called by The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) in Delhi. The CJP shared a video on social media showing its founder Abhijeet Dipke being detained with other leaders shortly after landing in the capital. The movement started in May after India's Chief Justice likened some unemployed young people to "cockroaches". Delhi police denied permission for the demonstration to take place, with tens of thousands of security personnel deployed and roads barricaded. But the CJP had insisted it would go ahead. BBC correspondent Azadeh Moshiri, on the ground in Delhi, explains what the latest protest is about.More on this story. title: Trump says Ukraine and Russia have agreed 'energy ceasefire'
content: Image source, Getty ImagesByTinshui YeungPublished11 October 2026, 15:46 BSTUpdated 1 hour agoDonald Trump has claimed that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire", with Kyiv saying it would support such a move but Moscow yet to comment.The US president insisted that it was "effective immediately" but provided no details.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky initially expressed surprise at the announcement, before saying Kyiv would support it if Moscow did. He also accused Russia of striking Ukrainian energy facilities after Trump's post.Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to curtailing revenue for Moscow's war machine - so Russia can fulfil a recently-struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.The diesel deal, temporarily undoing sanctions on Russian imports, is attracting growing criticism. Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin. European officials and some US politicians, including from Trump's Republican party, have said they do not support it.The deal is Trump's latest effort to lower domestic fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, having spent months grappling with the political consequences of the war with Iran which has pushed up global fuel prices, particularly those for diesel.That has soured Trump's standing with the American public, who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.Figure caption, Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?Zelensky said it was "news" to him that an energy truce was in effect in comments to news site Axios, before writing on social media that his officials "look forward to clear details of America's dialogue with Russia"."Ukraine is ready not to strike at Russian energy and we count on Russia's similar readiness and on the agreement of the president of the United States of America on this," he said.The BBC has asked the White House for further details.UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support.Zelensky later said Russia had hit a power plant in Kyiv with a drone, causing power cuts, followed by strikes on energy facilities in the north-eastern Kharkiv region."All of this happened after the president of the United States made his statement about an energy ceasefire," he said.For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure.Moscow said the installations it hits were legitimate targets because they supported Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".The attacks have disrupted energy supplies on both sides.Image source, Telegram/CrimeanwindImage caption, Huge plumes of smoke seen rising in the skies from the site where the Slavneft-Yanos oil refinery in Russia is located on 6 AugustEarlier on Sunday, UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC that the UK did not support it, while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas echoed Zelensky's criticism of it on Saturday.The deal has also attracted criticism from politicians of both main US parties.Seven senators, including three Democrats and four Republicans, have published a statement saying Trump's deal "runs directly counter" to a law that had explicitly banned Russian energy imports."Congress was clear: the US should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our Nato Allies," they said, urging the Trump administration to "reverse course".Republican Senator Thom Tillis, one of the seven, told NBC News that the deal "absolutely will" put American lives at risk.On Saturday Trump accused Zelensky of wanting to "make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries following the Ukrainian leader's criticism of the diesel deal.The US president suggested that it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president".Zelensky pledged to hold elections - despite them being suspended by the Ukrainian constitution during wartime - if Russia agreed to a 60-day total ceasefire.The Ukrainian president previously resisted calls from the US for fresh elections, pointing to complications with holding a vote in parts of the country that are active war zones or under Russian occupation.Trump, however, has repeatedly accused the Ukrainian leader of using the war to stay in power.Meanwhile, strikes and fighting on the ground continue in the four-year-long war.Six people were killed in attacks on two Ukrainian cities on Sunday, regional officials said.One person was killed in Russia's Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, while another man was killed in a drone attack in the Russian-occupied Donetsk region, officials said.Related topicsVolodymyr ZelenskyWar in UkraineMore on this story'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after Zelensky condemns diesel dealPublished21 hours agoTrump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a gift to PutinPublished1 day agoRussian strike on buses kills at least 30, say officials, as deadly attacks on Ukraine surgePublished3 days ago

title: Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport hit by second Houthi strike in two days
content: Figure caption, Watch: The scene at Riyadh international airport after strikeByTinshui YeungPublished11 October 2026, 17:41 BSTUpdated 4 minutes agoOne person has been killed and 11 injured in a second strike on the international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, officials have said.A Saudi military spokesman said a projectile had hit King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, causing a fire in one of its passenger halls. Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said in a statement on X that one person, a Pakistani resident, had been killed in the attack.It comes a day after a strike on the same airport killed 13 people and injured 308 others, following similar strikes earlier this week.The Houthis in Yemen said they were behind the attacks and warned airlines and passengers against using Saudi Arabian airports and airspace.The group said they had targeted the airport with a mix of ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones in the past 24 hours.They also attacked oil facilities and Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, their military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree said.He vowed to continue the "escalating operations deep inside Saudi Arabia", warning that all Saudi airports were potential targets apart from those in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.The Houthis have said they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war, as well as an air strike on the airport in Sanaa.On Sunday Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition, said air defences had intercepted a missile near the airport in Riyadh, while authorities were dealing with the fire caused by an "unknown projectile" that hit Passenger Hall No 4.US President Donald Trump has said the US would "make a decision" and "move very quickly" on whether to strike the Houthis, while UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting suggested the UK could "potentially" provide more support for Saudi Arabia.Riyadh airport attack another dangerous moment in already tense conflictPublished7 hours agoWho are the Houthis and what do they want?Published24 SeptemberSaturday's strike was the deadliest single attack on a Gulf Arab country since the war between Israel, the US and Iran began in February. The Saudi-led coalition vowed to respond, calling it a "war crime".Four Saudi nationals, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt were among the dead, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said on Sunday that an Indian man had succumbed to the injuries he sustained in the attack.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks and confirmed that a US citizen was killed in the strikes. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he was "appalled".The UK Foreign Office is advising against all travel to parts of Saudi Arabia, including areas within 10km (6.2 miles) of the border with Yemen, while other western embassies have warned their nationals about travel in the region.Houthi-run Al Masirah TV said "the Saudi enemy" had launched an air strike on Sanaa International Airport in Yemen's capital. A residential home in the city was also struck, killing a child and injuring six people, the media outlet reported. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the attacks and the BBC has been unable to verify this report.Abdullah Al-Alimi Bawazir, vice-president of Yemen's internationally recognised government, called for "decisive actions" from regional and international partners.Riyadh's airport was struck on Thursday, an attack that killed three Saudi nationals. The Houthis claimed responsibility and said they had used cruise missiles to target the airport.There were two other deadly attacks on Saudi airports in Abha and Riyadh in the two days prior to that. Image source, ReutersImage caption, Smoke and flames seen at King Khalid airport in Riyadh on 8 OctoberThe latest uptick in violence comes after a temporary ceasefire between the Houthis and Saudi-led forces, brokered in 2022, collapsed in July.The conflict worsened after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive, prompting Saudi strikes. Yemeni pro-government forces later said they had secured the regions.The Houthis currently control around a quarter of Yemeni territory and as much as 80% of the country's population. The Iran-backed armed group hopes to eventually seize complete control.Saudi Arabia fears this would lead to the establishment of an Iranian satellite state on its southern border.Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told his Saudi Arabian counterpart on Sunday that his country was ready to provide assistance to "facilitate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen", referring to the Houthi administration.Related topicsHouthis Saudi ArabiaYemenSaudi Arabian-led intervention in YemenRiyadhMore on this storyYemeni military says it has 'secured' Red Sea waterwayPublished5 days agoInside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for controlPublished27 SeptemberHow escalating Saudi oil crisis could drive up prices everywherePublished16 September

title: Poland detains man suspected of planning assassination of PM Donald Tusk
content: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Donald Tusk thanked the police for "swift and decisive action"ByGeorge WrightPublished5 hours agoPoland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a man accused of plotting an assassination attack against him and his defence minister has been detained.The interior ministry earlier reported that police had received credible information about possible attacks against Tusk and Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz.Polish security services convened a special meeting on Sunday after receiving information about the planned attacks, with a spokesman saying officials were treating the threat as "deadly serious".Tusk thanked the police for "swift and decisive action" in arresting the suspect.The suspect was arrested in the Lower Silesia region and was a Polish national, Jacek Dobrzynski, a spokesman for the Special Services Co-ordinator told local media."In this case we are talking about a strong likelihood that these threats could actually be carried out," he said.The plan was uncovered when an email with information about the potential attack was forwarded to police by the State Protection Service, which is responsible for ministers' security, Interior Ministry spokeswoman Karolina Galecka said.Tusk has been Polish prime minister since 2023, having previously held the office from 2007 to 2014.He served as president of the European Council from 2014 to 2019.Related topicsEuropePolandDonald TuskMore on this storyPoland stabbings driven by online glorification of violence, Tusk saysPublished7 hours ago

title: Dozens of gold prospectors killed in strikes on Egypt-Sudan border, rights group says
content: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, File photo of gold prospectors in northern SudanByAleks PhillipsPublished52 minutes agoAt least 72 civilians who had been prospecting for gold in a border region of Sudan have been killed in air strikes, a regional rights group says.Emergency Lawyers, based in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, said jets targeted the so-called artisanal miners at a popular gold mining sites in Sudan's River Nile state on Saturday.Neither the Egyptian government nor the de facto Sudanese authorities have so far commented. Cairo has previously faced accusations of deadly strikes on gold prospectors as part of a crackdown on illicit activity along its southern border.Emergency Lawyers noted the previous alleged attacks and said they represented not only a violation of Sudan's sovereign territory but demonstrated the government's lack of control over the region."The deliberate targeting of unarmed civilians violates international humanitarian law and the right to life," it said in a statement on Sunday. "These acts may constitute war crimes."It noted that its death toll was provisional and could rise. The Paris-based Sudan Tribune reported that the death toll could far exceed the number reported by Emergency Lawyers, citing a survivor of Saturday's attack who said many more people had been injured.Eyewitnesses said the attack began around 06:00 local time (04:00 GMT), with the aircraft firing more than five missiles directly at the miners' camps, destroying them and excavation pits with people still inside, the newspaper wrote.The Sudan Tribune reported claims in June that Egyptian forces had used drones and artillery to target artisanal mining sites in the same region, killing several, after sporadic incidents of Egyptian border guards of burning equipment, torching temporary shelters, and firing live ammunition to disperse mine workers.Days later, Egypt's border agency announced that it and the military had begun a sweeping security campaign along the border to foil illegal migration, drug smuggling and illegal mining.At the same time, Sudan's de facto leader announced an investigation into the alleged strikes, which were said to have killed dozens.Gold lies at the core of the border tensions. Sudan's ongoing civil war has led to a surge in artisanal mining - an often risky practice conducted by civilians with rudimentary tools and without official permission - particularly in remote areas near its borders. Gold-rich areas such as those in River Nile state lie along porous borders in terrain historically associated with cross-border smuggling routes, with artisanally mined gold potentially feeding into those channels. Egypt's border force said in June that it had seized 86 tonnes of gold ore along with amateur prospecting equipment.Artisanal mining has also reportedly continued in Sudan's conflict zones and smuggled gold may be a source of income for armed insurgent groups.This has raised concerns of illicit Sudanese gold undermining the legitimate Egyptian gold market.Related topicsSudanEgyptAfricaMiningMore on this storyA simple guide to what is happening in SudanPublished13 November 2025

title: Homes and bridges swept away as fresh floods hit Nepal
content: Figure caption, Flash flood washes building complex in central NepalBy Navin Singh KhadkaEnvironment correspondent, BBC World ServicePublished11 October 2026, 13:03 BSTA major river in Nepal has flooded, sweeping away houses, bridges and damaging a part of hydropower station, authorities have said.Around 50 people have been rescued from along the bank of the Budhi Gandaki River in the central Gorkha district, the army confirmed. No casualties have been reported yet, however five people are missing.A video of the flood shows the moment raging waters sweep down a valley and wash away an entire building complex.Nepal is on high alert and still trying to recover from catastrophic floods that hit its border towns with Tibet two months ago, leaving more than 1,400 people dead and thousands missing.Sunday's flood tore through the Gorkha district as children and communities prepared to mark the first day of the Dashain festival, a major moment in the Nepali calendar.Families have been forced to flee their homes, with many facing uncertainty over where they will find safe shelter and access to essential supplies.The flood swept away about a dozen houses and several suspension bridges, while a hydroelectric project was damaged, carrying some of the construction equipment away, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said.Within a couple of hours, the river's water levels at one location had risen from two metres (6ft 5in) to nearly 8.5m (27ft 9in), officials said.Binod Parajuli, a meteorologist who works with the Nepalese government, said: "Our hydrological station was swept away and we are not getting any data from that location."However, experts say the debris-flow is much smaller and travelled more slowly than the devastating flash floods in August.What caused the latest flood is still unclear. Some say a landslide may have blocked the river or its tributary for some time, causing the dammed water to burst out, while others say locals upstream saw an ice-avalanche.Save the Children is mobilising an emergency team to respond to Sunday's flood."Children's lives have been ripped apart in an instant yet again", the charity's director in Nepal, Tara Chettry, said."We are yet to see the full scale of the damage, but they may have lost their homes, schools and communities. Many children in Gorkha will still be in shock and distress after the mega floods in August, barely having a chance to get back on their feet."The Budhi Gandaki is a tributary of the Trishuli river, downstream from another tributary where a glacier collapse caused the previous disaster.Related topicsNepalMore on this storyMany Nepalis swept away in the floods aren't officially dead, leaving families in limboPublished5 days ago

title: Yandex: Ukraine strikes data centre in third attack on Russian tech giant
content: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Yandex's data centres have been targeted three times this week - like this one in Sasovo on ThursdayByHafsa KhalilPublished11 October 2026, 13:50 BSTUpdated 7 hours agoYandex has been forced to pause its operations at a data centre near Moscow after the facility was damaged in a Ukrainian drone strike - the third attack on the Russian tech giant's sites this week.The company - dubbed "Russia's Google" - said no one was injured at the centre in Vladimir, east of the capital, but some of its services were unavailable to users.Earlier this week, Yandex said it was struggling to maintain its services after two of its five data centres were hit in Ukrainian strikes.Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between them continues in its fifth year following Russia's full-scale invasion. Kyiv said it was targeting places that provide revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the attacks could force Russia to divert its resources to repair the damage at Yandex.Sunday's attack came hours after US President Donald Trump warned that Ukraine should "damn well stop" attacking Russia's oil refineries so Moscow could release more diesel to the global market - a deal that has drawn criticism from Europe and sparked a diplomatic row with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky.'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after Zelensky condemns diesel dealPublished20 hours agoAnalysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel pricesPublished1 day agoYandex confirmed on Telegram that its data centre in Vladimir had been damaged and that operations had been "completely suspended", although it said it was working to restore connectivity.The other strikes against Yandex facilities were on Thursday in Sasovo and Friday in in Kaluga, south-west of Moscow, causing problems for some of its services, such as its AI chatbot and smart home devices.The tech company - which also runs a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people - said at the time that its data centres were critical for the normal operation of its services, and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.Meanwhile, Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued through the weekend.The State Emergency Service of Ukraine said six people were injured in Russian attacks overnight on four districts in its south-eastern Dnipropetrovsk region.On Saturday, at least 20 people including four children were killed in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia, local officials confirmed.Russia has previously also struck Ukrainian data centres, causing internet outages and prompting some firms to move their servers abroad.Related topicsRussiaWar in UkraineMore on this storyNord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to UkrainePublished1 day agoRussian strikes and approaching winter force some in Kyiv to pack bags and fleePublished2 days agoFear and disruption for Ukraine's rail passengers as Russia escalates drone attacksPublished5 days ago

title: Orangutans released back into Borneo forest after devastating fires
content: Figure caption, Watch: Endangered orangutans released back into the wild after after Borneo firesByAleks PhillipsPublished4 hours agoEight orangutans have been released back into the wild in Borneo after they were taken into captivity when their habitat was threatened by wildfires over the summer.Three mothers, their three daughters and two adult males were freed in a reserve in the west of the island on Friday, International Animal Rescue Indonesia (Yiari) and the forestry ministry said.Indonesian authorities rescued 46 orangutans from fires in August and September.
