Wildfires in the region are usual for the country's dry season but intensified this year.The apes are critically endangered. Around 104,000 orangutans remain in Borneo and Sumatra, down from more than 230,000 a century ago, according to conservation group WWF.While Indonesia is among many countries to grapple with wildfires each summer, this year's were more intense due to the El Niño ocean warming phenomenon, which makes weather patterns more volatile and intense.Yiari CEO Karmele Llano Sanchez said relocating the eight orangutans to the reserve was a "necessary step" when their habitats became unsafe.Among them was Mama Nopi and her offspring Nopi, Naufal and Nopan, who had been surviving in a coconut and rubber plantation before their rescue in early September, Yiari said.Fires had incinerated the surrounding forestry, restricting their access to food and bringing them closer to humans.Image source, Muffidz Ma'sum/Yiara/MoEFImage caption, The apes were all rescued from wildfires over the summer that threatened their habitatsMama Lifa and her child Lifa were found in a patch of acacia trees entirely surrounded by oil palm plantations.The degradation of their habitat by wildfires as well as a lack of food sources prompted their rescue in mid-September.Mama Man and her baby, Man, had been monitored by animal rescuers since June, when they were found living in a plantation area adjacent to a small patch of forest.Fires that spread near to the site restricted their roaming area further, leaving them without a safe route to other forestry. The threat of exposure to the blazes led to them being evacuated in early September, Yiara said.The reserve these orangutans were released into was chosen because it there is food and water available and it is connected to other forested areas.Yiari's Argitoe Ranting said: "We want to ensure that rescued orangutans are not simply moved from one place to another, but actually have a chance to survive in their natural habitat."Image source, Muffidz Ma'sum/Yiara/MoEFImage caption, The orangutans were moved to a reserve connected with other forests and with plenty of natural resourcesLast month, the International Union for Conservation of Nature warned that wildfires were burning in habitats containing 52% of Borneo's orangutan population.It says a large portion of the ape's habitat will become inhospitable to them if climate change continues at its current pace.This year's El Niño has become the strongest on record and is expected to have a knock-on effect on the climate into next year.Experts have also pointed to land-clearing practices used to make room for plantations as another factor facilitating the spread of wildfires in Indonesia, with naturally fire-resistant forests replaced by less dense and shaded vegetation.That the orangutan's original habitats had been burned and fragmented to the point they could no longer sustain the primates was the main driving factor behind relocating them, Yiara said.Figure caption, In August a weak orangutan was found lying on the ground in Borneo as wildfires blazed through the islandRelated topicsIndonesiaOrangutansAnimal welfareConservationWildfiresBorneoMore on this storyWildfires came 'worryingly' close to animal sanctuaryPublished1 day agoWatch: How one orangutan braved new bridge to unite his split communityPublished25 AprilToxic wildfire haze spreads across South East Asia as 'super' El Niño intensifiesPublished3 September

title: Poland stabbings driven by online glorification of violence, Tusk says
content: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, A 37-year-old caretaker was killed at a primary school in a town north of Warsaw this weekByGeorge WrightPublished7 hours agoThree violent attacks at Polish schools this week were driven by the "glorification of violence" online, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.The attacks have left one woman dead and others injured, including children."These are very often spontaneous actions inspired by online activity," Tusk said on Sunday, during a crisis meeting with security services. Police have arrested 117 people across the country for possession knives or other weapons, or for threatening to attack schools or fellow students, after searching tens of thousands of schools.A woman was arrested on Saturday after injuring three people while attacking a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in the capital, Warsaw.It came a day after thousands of police visited schools across Poland, following two stabbing attacks earlier in the week, one of which led to the killing of a female caretaker."We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale," Tusk said on Sunday. "In the past years and months, we have noted - globally and in Poland - a rise in the fascination with violence," he added.The prime minister said the attacks were acts of "nihilistic violence" associated with the extreme right."Some of the people detained are active in the ultraright environment," he said, adding that police had noticed a rise in online searches of Nazi content as well as of "mass killers who have become idols online".On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student attacked and injured nine people at a vocational school in the central Polish province of Mazovian.A day later, the 37-year-old caretaker was killed after a 15-year-old entered a primary school in Leszczydół-Nowiny, north of Warsaw.Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński also said a 17-year-old was detained in the town of Sierpc, north-west of Warsaw, after allegedly stating "on school grounds that he planned to do something... dangerous - that he intended to harm someone".Thousands of Polish ‌police officers visited schools nationwide to try to reassure pupils after the stabbings sparked rumours of a "Bloody Friday" of more attacks stemming from a supposed online challenge.Meanwhile, Polish security services convened a special meeting on Sunday after receiving information about a potential attack on Tusk and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, a spokesperson said.A special services spokesman said officials were treating the threat as "deadly serious".Related topicsEuropePolandMore on this storyWoman injures three people in third Poland school knife attack in a weekPublished1 day agoCaretaker killed and two teachers injured in knife attack at Poland schoolPublished3 days ago

title: Djibouti boat capsize: Children among 139 dead with 84 still missing, UN says
content: Image source, International Organization for MigrationImage caption, IOM workers receiving migrants near Guhere, north of the port town of ObockByHafsa KhalilPublished11 October 2026, 13:05 BSTUpdated 5 hours agoAt least 139 migrants including 15 children have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the UN's migration office has said.The boat had been travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people aboard when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Around 82 people were rescued, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said.IOM's Djibouti mission chief Alexandre Coissac called the tragedy a "stark reminder" of the dangers migrants face when seeking a new life elsewhere.Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa make the perilous journey each year hoping to reach Gulf countries for safety and work, the agency says.The organisation revised its toll from 109 on Sunday after 30 more bodies were recovered."This is a devastating loss of life," Coissac said. "Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives."Local authorities are also arranging burials for those who have died, while the survivors - all Ethiopian nationals - have medical care readily available to them.Yemen remains engulfed in a devastating civil war that has lasted more than a decade. Despite this conflict - and growing instability across the wider region - migrants still cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen driven by poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change.Since 10 September, the IOM said its Displacement Tracking Matrix had observed more than 20,000 "movements" from Ethiopia to Djibouti.Image caption, The boat was travelling from Djibouti to YemenIOM said it was providing assistance to 64 of the survivors at its response centre in Obock, including healthcare and support to "restore contact with their families".The UN agency was working in "close collaboration" with local authorities to help migrants and "prevent deaths at sea and on land", it added.More than 900 migrants died or went missing taking the same route in 2025, during an 18% increase in the number of people attempting the journey, according to IOM statistics.In March 2026, nine people were killed and 45 went missing following a similar incident as Thursday's.The conflict in Yemen has also displaced more than 130,000 people across the country, the UN refugee agency said last month. Thousands of Yemenis have fled to Djibouti to escape the civil war between Houthi fighters and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.Djibouti is a tiny former French colony that sits just across the Gulf of Aden from Yemen.Related topicsDjiboutiYemenMigrationShipwrecksAfricaEthiopiaMore on this storyChildren brave snipers and mortars to go to school near Yemen front line Published5 days agoInside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for controlPublished27 SeptemberDozens of migrants die in boat capsize off YemenPublished4 August 2025

title: Pope Leo XIV to have surgery after nodule found on lung
content: Figure caption, Pope Leo announces he will undergo surgery for early-stage lung noduleByRorey BosottiPublished11 October 2026, 11:53 BSTUpdated 9 hours agoPope Leo XIV has announced he will be operated on "in the coming days" after a nodule was found on his lung during a medical check-up."The doctors found an early, well-localised nodule on my lung," he told the public during his weekly Sunday prayers in St Peter's Square in Rome.The 71-year-old said his medical team "believe it would be right to intervene" and he had agreed to the operation, while reassuring pilgrims that the mass was "well-contained" and caught "at an early stage".The pontiff's admission that he would need surgery comes nearly a year-and-a-half after he succeeded the late Pope Francis, who also experienced issues with his lungs that required hospital treatment.Leo concluded his Angelus prayer by thanking everyone for their "spiritual closeness" and said he entrusted himself to their prayers.Holy See Press Office spokesman Matteo Bruni told the media that "the operation is scheduled for the first days of next week".He added that the Pope is expected to take about a week to recover.Vatican News, the Holy See's news portal, said the operation will take place at Gemelli Hospital in Rome.The hospital set up a special Papal suite following the failed assassination attempt on Pope John Paul II's life in May 1981, which is still in use today.Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her "personal solidarity" with the Pope as he "faces the ordeal ahead in the coming days".Her sentiments were echoed by Italian President Sergio Mattarella, who offered his "sincerest wishes for a peaceful recovery and a speedy and full return to health".Isaac Herzog, the president of Israel, also wished the pontiff "a full and speedy recovery".The Pope, born Robert Francis Prevost, is the 267th occupant of the throne of St Peter – the first US citizen to do so.He was ordained in 1982 and spent years as a missionary in Peru, where he is remembered as a figure who worked with marginalised communities.During Sunday's service, the Pope confirmed his upcoming visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November will still go ahead.The Archbishop of Montevideo, Daniel Sturla, said preparations for his tour will continue with "greater enthusiasm" as he called for prayers for his recovery.A lung nodule is a small lump of tissue that is usually detected following an X-ray or CT scan of the chest, according to the NHS.Most nodules do not cause other symptoms.Related topicsPope Leo XIVRoman Catholic ChurchVatican CityMore on this storyMission is to preach peace, says Pope in response to Trump attacksPublished5 MayPope warns against 'losing humanity' to AI machinesPublished25 SeptemberTrump's rift with Pope is playing out in public - it's costing him valuable supportPublished15 April

title: Justice Department investigating television networks over Trump pool coverage
content: Image source, EPAImage caption, The row over the White House pool affected live TV coverage of Trump events last monthByMadeline HalpertPublished11 October 2026, 01:49 BSTUpdated 06:05 BSTThe US Department of Justice (DoJ) has said it is investigating several TV networks over whether they broke federal competition laws when they recently suspended pool coverage of Donald Trump. Last month, five networks paused their presidential coverage for several days in response to the Trump administration withdrawing the credentials of reporters from CNN, MS Now and Politico.The DoJ asked ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News to hand over communications related to the pool and said the boycott could violate the Sherman Act, referring to a law that bars companies from engaging in monopolistic business practices.Pool members usually share their material with the wider media.A DoJ spokesperson said: "The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these ​news organisations have violated the antitrust laws."The television networks have not yet commented.Trump blocked CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House last month after accusing the organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his team.The White House later reinstated their access following a judge's ruling. The three outlets had sued the Trump administration, arguing the restricted access violated their First Amendment rights.The First Amendment forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.The Trump administration has taken a number of legal actions against news publications in the US, including lawsuits over coverage of the president.In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool, which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.The same month, the Trump administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.Related topicsMediaPress freedomDonald TrumpMore on this storyCNN, MS NOW and Politico file lawsuit against Trump's White House banPublished22 SeptemberMajor US outlets suspend shared Trump coverage in protest at media banPublished22 September

title: Expedition hopes to find aviator Amelia Earhart's plane on remote island
content: Image source, Purdue UniversityImage caption, The research team departed Kiribati's capital on Wednesday and hope to arrive at the suspected wreck site by MondayByAleks PhillipsPublished10 October 2026A team of researchers are on their way to a remote island to inspect what they think could be the plane wreckage of famed aviator Amelia Earhart.The group, from the US-based Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) and Purdue University, are expected to arrive at Nikumaroro Island in the Pacific Ocean by Monday in the hopes of solving the mystery of her disappearance.The American pioneer vanished while attempting to circumnavigate the globe in 1937, spawning decades of speculation on her fate.The team are aiming to find what has been called the Taraia Object, first spotted sitting on the edge of a lagoon off Nikumaroro in satellite imagery in 2020.Purdue University said the object had since been confirmed to have been visible in aerial photography of the area dating back to 1938.The researchers are currently roughly halfway through their journey to the remote atoll aboard the Marin Mainiku, a Kiribati National Shipping Line vessel.They departed the capital of Kiribati on Wednesday to begin the 830-mile journey to Nikumaroro, which is also part of the multi-island country.When they eventually arrive, they will have to navigate through a narrow gap created in the atoll's reef by the British in 1963 - the last time the island was inhabited."Finding Amelia Earhart's Electra aircraft would be the discovery of a lifetime," Richard Pettigrew, head of the ALI and the expedition lead, said.Image source, Archaeological Legacy InstituteImage caption, A satellite image of the so-called Taraia Object in a lagoon on NikumaroroEarhart had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her Electra twin-engine plane when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea on 2 July 1937.From there, she and her navigator Fred Noonan had planned to travel towards Hawaii and then finally back to California.But her plane vanished without a trace while trying to reach Howland Island, a remote, uninhabited coral island near Nikumaroro, to refuel.Earhart's disappearance spawned numerous theories - from a simple crash due to fuel exhaustion to more elaborate claims of interference.The official explanation is that the plane suffered communication problems while the two struggled to find the island, and Earhart eventually crashed into the ocean when she ran out of fuel.While this version of events is largely accepted, no physical evidence has ever been recovered.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Amelia Earhart disappeared over the Pacific Ocean while piloting her Electra plane in 1937One theory is that Earhart unintentionally navigated to Nikumaroro, where she ditched her plane and died a castaway.Images of the so-called Taraia Object show what could be the remnants of a small aircraft sitting in shallow waters.But some - including rival explorers - have expressed scepticism that this could be a plane, let alone Earhart's.Ric Gillespie, who specialises in recovering historic aircraft wrecks, told news agency Reuters that the object looked like a tree that had fallen from the atoll into the nearby water."I'd love to find that airplane. It ain't gonna happen," he said.The researchers en route to the island credit Gillespie with previously finding evidence of a human presence on the atoll in the 1930s and forensic analysis of skeletal remains found there in the 1940s they say lend credence to their theory.But Gillespie suspects Earhart's plane had likely broken apart and its fragments carried into the depths of the Pacific long ago.Previous attempts to find her Electra have also come up short.In 2024, a group of researchers said they may have found it lying around 4,877m (16,000ft) below the surface near Howland Island through sonar imaging - but this was later confirmed to be a rock formation.Similarly, an expedition in 2019, conducted by the marine archaeologist who discovered the Titanic wreck, to investigate a photograph of what might have been a landing gear protruding from the water near Nikumaroro also failed to find anything.Related topicsAviation accidents and incidentsKiribatiPacific OceanMore on this storyTrump to declassify files over aviation pioneer Amelia EarhartPublished27 September 2025Expedition seeks Earhart answersPublished3 July 20121933: Amelia Earhart talks about her transatlantic crossingPublished28 May 2024

title: CJP at Jantar Mantar: Delhi sees more protests as freed 'cockroach' group's leaders vow to continue fight
content: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Hundreds of protesters continued to be detained in Delhi on SundayByGeeta Pandey and Zoya Mateen, BBC DelhiPublished11 October 2026, 07:02 BSTUpdated 12:11 BSTIndia's Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has vowed to continue its protest seeking the resignation of top election official even as the nation's capital sees demonstrations for a second day, with thousands of security personnel deployed and roads barricaded.Abhijeet Dipke - who began the movement in May after India's Chief Justice likened some jobless young people to "cockroaches" - and other leaders were arrested on arrival in Delhi on Saturday. They were freed on Sunday.Dipke said "the CJP will neither back down nor be intimidated" in his first comments after his release.Media reports said 7,000 protesters were detained and released on Saturday, with hundreds detained on Sunday.The CJP - which is not registered as a political party in India - is seeking electoral reforms just months before crucial state elections.It has also demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists - which the Election Commission has denied.On Sunday morning, Dipke and two other senior CJP leaders - Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were set free by a magistrate's court "on the condition that they will not engage in breach of peace for one year", police said.After his release, Dipke posted on X: "Modi, as PM, is an embarrassment to India."He said he was going to his village to attend the funeral of his grandmother, who died around the time of his arrest. He added that "the CJP will neither back down nor be intimidated". Ranka and Das later told a news conference that the condition did not mean they could not protest."Peaceful protest is our constitutional right and Jantar Mantar is a desginated protest site, so this doesn't mean we can't do peaceful protest," Ranka said. "Breach of peace is done by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and CEC Gyanesh Kumar," he said, adding that the CJP will continue to protest.Saturday saw dramatic scenes as police officials boarded the flight to detain Dipke, Das and Ranka as their plane landed.Figure caption, 'Cockroach' leaders say they have been detained ahead of marchFor a second day in a row on Sunday, much of central Delhi had roads barricaded, offices, shops and restaurants shut and internet services curtailed.In Connaught Place, one of Delhi's busiest shopping and entertainment hubs, there were rows upon rows of bright yellow police barricades, guarded by thousands of police and paramilitary personnel.Protesters were vastly outnumbered by security personnel and the BBC has witnessed many detentions.Some were put onto buses before being driven away. Some could be seen peering through the windows, others trying to push their way out while shouting "Gyanesh must go!" At one point, an entire bus reverberated with similar chants.Every now and then, small groups of protesters managed to slip past the barricades and sprint through the streets, with police personnel chasing after them. Within moments, they were surrounded, detained and, in some instances, dragged across the road, before being bundled into waiting buses.The most dramatic moment came during the detention of activist Neha Bora, external, who was chased by police personnel before being caught and detained.Some protesters also said they were feeling a little uncertain. One of them told the BBC that the absence of the CJP's top leadership on the ground was beginning to affect the movement's momentum."Without them, we're feeling a little lost," the protester admitted, before quickly adding: "But that doesn't mean we'll stop our fight."Image caption, Security forces have been deployed across DelhiThe CJP had called for a protest on Saturday at Jantar Mantar - the road that the demonstrators had occupied for weeks earlier this summer seeking education reforms.Police had refused them permission and the city was in a virtual lockdown with unprecedented curbs in place to thwart the protesters from reaching the venue.At least 45 metro stations were closed and Delhi's main railway stations were shut with major train services cancelled. Many protesters attempting to travel from outside were de-boarded en route. Internet was also curtailed in central Delhi for the entire day.After the police detained the CJP leaders and other activists, lawyers and students leaders, the CJP called for more protests on Sunday.On Sunday, the Indian Supreme Court held a special hearing to deal with complaints of shutdowns and detentions.The court ordered the government to restore the internet, and ensure that metro and rail services functioned normally, unless there were a disturbance to public order. The court also said that free movement of people should be permitted and there should be no illegal detention.Figure caption, Watch: Why have hundreds of 'cockroach' protesters been detained in DelhiWhy are people protesting?The row centres on a mammoth exercise to update electoral rolls nationwide. The commission has said it's a routine exercise to weed out dead, duplicate or ineligible voters.At least 130 million voter names have been purged from the rolls so far and in many states, the exercise has been shrouded in controversy, with tens of thousands of people alleging they have been wrongly removed.The CJP - and opposition parties - accuse Kumar of favouring Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the way the electoral rolls are being updated.The Election Commission and the BJP have denied this.The CJP first emerged as a major protest movement during weeks of demonstrations over the summer demanding education reforms.Dipke, who previously worked with the opposition Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), had just completed a master's degree at Boston University when he wrote on X in May: "What if all cockroaches come together?" Chief Justice Surya Kant says his cockroach comments were misinterpreted.But Dipke's post went viral and the CJP was born. Momentum built around the movement which tapped into anger over unemployment, exam paper leaks and government accountability.Their five-week-long protest ended in celebration for the protesters in July after the resignation of India's education minister.Related topicsIndiaDelhiMore on this storyMeet India's feisty Gen Z protester who is taking on ModiPublished2 days agoLockdown-like scenes at usually bustling central Delhi marketsPublished1 day agoIndia's 'cockroach' protesters are back - this time asking poll chief to resignPublished2 October

title: Christa Pike discharged from hospital 10 days after failed execution
content: Image source, ReutersByGrace Eliza GoodwinPublished10 October 2026US death row inmate Christa Pike has been discharged from hospital following her botched execution at the end of last month, her lawyers have said.Pike, 50, has been sent back to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years and is continuing to receive medical care, according to a statement from her lawyers on Saturday.She survived two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September, which left her in a critical condition.Pike regained consciousness earlier this week and began speaking - stunning experts, medical staff and her lawyers.Her case is now in uncharted territory as she is thought to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike'sPublished2 OctoberI interviewed Christa Pike 20 years ago - I can't stop thinking about herPublished3 OctoberWhat happened in Christa Pike's failed US execution, and how did she survive? Published3 days agoPike's lawyers said in their statement that she was "grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances".It is unclear what medical care Pike is receiving now that she is back in prison but her lawyers previously said she faced a "long road to recovery". The Tennessee Department of Correction is yet to say why the execution did not go as planned, though it has defended the method it used.Figure caption, How widely used is the death penalty in the US?At a court hearing on Wednesday, Tennessee Assistant Attorney General Will Ayers told the judge he did not know whether the state intends to try to execute her again.The judge ordered the state to preserve all evidence related to the failed injections. That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.Shipp was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.Pike was the first woman scheduled to be executed in the state of Tennessee in over 200 years. Her lawyers have spent decades appealing her case. In the days leading up to her scheduled execution, both the US Supreme Court and Tennessee Governor Bill Lee declined to block the execution. Since it failed, Pike's lawyers have renewed their calls for her sentence to be commuted to life in prison without the possibility of parole. Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and ShippPike lost consciousness and was taken to a local hospital following her botched execution. Her legal team believed for days that she was brain dead and expected her to be taken off life support at any moment.Pike eventually woke up and began talking again on Tuesday - her lawyer Randy Spivey said her first words were "Where am I?" and "Who are you?"At a press conference on Wednesday, her lawyers said she was shackled to the bed and suffering from pneumonia and significant swelling on her arms, while also being unable to swallow."We don't know the toll all of this will take" Spivey said of her mental health, adding that Pike felt "angry and confused".Related topicsTennesseeMore on this storyChrista Pike now walking after failed US execution, lawyer tells BBCPublished3 days agoChrista Pike has 'profound' health turnaround after botched execution, lawyers sayPublished2 days ago

title: Headmaster detained after BBC investigation into alleged sexual abuse of students
content: Image source, BBC IndonesiaImage caption, Ex-headmaster Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to students as Abah, has been accused of sexual abuseByEndang Nurdin, Rebecca Henschke, BBC Eye Investigations and BBC IndonesiaPublished10 October 2026A former headmaster of an Islamic boarding school in Indonesia has been named as a suspect in a sexual abuse investigation and detained by police, following a BBC Eye report.Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to students as Abah, led the Abul Barokat boarding school on the island of Lombok.Police reopened the case after the BBC World Service revealed accusations of sexual abuse against him, and documented how former students had gathered evidence in an effort to bring the allegations to the authorities. The story sparked public outrage and led to 12 more former students giving testimony to police.Warning: This story contains details of sexual assaultCatching My Teacher Two ex-students expose sexual abuse by teachers at Islamic boarding schools in IndonesiaWatch on iPlayerListen on SoundsOutside the UK, you can watch Catching My Teacher on YouTube, external.The student detectivesCentral to the BBC Eye investigation were former students Ziadatur Rahmah, known as Zia, and Sukma Rohana Fajar.They launched their own investigation after Zia told a former classmate, Yusron Azzahidi, that the headteacher had sexually assaulted her when she was 17. The pair had been star pupils at the school. By the time Zia confided in Yusron, she was studying in Cairo, Egypt, while he was in Jakarta. Yusron suggested they gather evidence to support Zia's allegation. Speaking to former classmates, they spoke to Sukma, who alleges that Abah attempted to rape her at the school.Yusron compiled a seven-page document detailing the allegations, and they gave it to representatives of Nahdlatul Wathan Diniyah Islamiyah (NWDI), the organisation that ran the school.Thinking the school would support them, the students say that instead, they were pressured to withdraw their accusations.In a secretly recorded phone call, Abah pleaded with Yusron to protect him and his reputation."Cover the shame of your teacher. Everyone makes mistakes, my child," Abah said.Abah also contacted Zia, who secretly recorded their conversation and shared it with the BBC. In the recording, Abah is heard apologising, but pleads with her to remain silent.Following the BBC investigation, Abah held a news conference where he denied all the allegations. He did not deny that the voice heard in the recorded calls was his, but said the recordings were not confessions.Sukma told the BBC she had been forced to sign a document saying her allegations were lies. She later secretly recorded a conversation with Abah's wife, known to students as Umi. In the recording, Umi tells Sukma that the document was intended to protect "her good name".The former students eventually resumed their efforts to seek justice, with support from lawyer Joko Jumadi, who has experience in similar cases.Figure caption, Watch: BBC tracks down abusive teacher secretly released earlyMore students come forwardThe day after the BBC investigation was published, parents arrived at the school to collect their children, with some travelling from other islands.One mother said she had begun crying when she heard the news, thinking about her daughter."I'm moving her right now," she said. "I absolutely want my child to leave this school."Yusron said he and Zia, who recently got married, were overwhelmed by the response from former students."It was beyond what we expected," he said. "So many people contacted us - on Instagram, WhatsApp. They contacted me and Zia directly, and lots of them were saying, 'I'm a victim too'."Police interviewed Zia and Sukma, along with the 12 other former students who came forward with allegations of abuse."They thought they were the only ones - and it's been really shocking for them to learn, like I did, that they weren't alone," Zia said.Sukma said she felt relieved and grateful that the allegations are now being taken seriously."It's not about revenge. It's more the acknowledgement that what he did was wrong. I'm waiting for the day when he admits that himself," she told the BBC.Abah has resigned from the school and has said he will respect the legal process.The BBC contacted Abah and his wife during its original investigation, but they did not respond at the time.NWDI denied trying to cover up the allegations and said it was investigating them internally. It said it had a duty to protect the organisation from being tarnished by the alleged actions of individuals.In the wake of the BBC investigation, NWDI vowed to ensure such abuse never happened again and said it would safeguard the rights of students who came forward.Related topicsIndonesiaSexual violenceAsia

title: Woman injures three people in third Poland school knife attack in a week
content: Image source, Agencja Wyborcza.pl via ReutersByRorey BosottiPublished10 October 2026A woman has been arrested after injuring three people in a third knife attack recorded at schools in Poland this week.The 21-year-old used a "dangerous object" to attack a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in the capital, Warsaw, police told news agencies PAP and AP.It comes a day after thousands of police visited schools across Poland, following two stabbing attacks earlier in the week, one of which led to the killing of a female caretaker.A Warsaw police spokesperson said they could not confirm whether the latest incident was related to the two previous attacks.Authorities told local media that the 17-year-old injured on Saturday had been taken to hospital, but her condition was not life-threatening. Two other women aged 17 and 24, who had gone in to submit enrolment documents, were also injured, Poland's state news agency reported.Police told local media that the suspected attacker was a student at the school and initial findings suggested that she did not know the three victims.Schools in Poland had been stepping up security following knife attacks at schools across the country on 7 and 8 October. Polish police said they had detained 76 people after deploying to schools across the country."When it comes to the safety of Polish children and peace in our schools, there is no room for compromise," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said ahead of the operation.Local media, citing a police spokesperson, reported authorities had information to suggest incidents this past week could be related to an internet challenge.On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student attacked and injured nine people at a vocational school in the central Polish province of Mazovian.A day later, a 37-year-old caretaker was killed after a 15-year-old entered a primary school in Leszczydół-Nowiny, north of Warsaw.Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński also said a 17-year-old was detained in the town of Sierpc, north-west of Warsaw, after allegedly stating "on school grounds that he planned to do something... dangerous - that he intended to harm someone".Related topicsPolandKnife crime

title: Nobel peace laureate says US sanctions on ICC 'unacceptable'
content: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The South African former ICC judge was awarded the prize on FridayByGeorge WrightPublished10 October 2026Navi Pillay, the winner of this year's Nobel Peace Prize, has called US sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) "unheard of" and "unacceptable".The South African former ICC judge was awarded the prize on Friday "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.US President Donald Trump expressed his disatisfaction with the pick and hours later the US unveiled sweeping sanctions in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it described as a "rogue" institution.The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.Pillay, speaking via video link during an event at the Nobel Peace Center in Oslo on Saturday, said: "There is so much tension and anxiety over the continued existence of international courts, mainly the International Criminal Court in The Hague."Most importantly, sanctions have been announced by one country against the judges, just for the judicial orders they issue. This is unheard of, unacceptable." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier said the sanctions - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.The US has already sanctioned 17 ICC judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to inhibit its ability to operate financially.However, the US has provided a six-month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns.The Trump administration claims that the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty.It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted.UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar".The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in saying they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions.Figure caption, Watch: Who is Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay?Pillay, 85, also served as UN rights chief, taking part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza.Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country's fifth Peace Prize winner - following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu."If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked after receiving the prize, a reference to last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition figure María Corina Machado, deciding to gift her prize to the US president.Trump called the announcement of Pillay as 2026's winner "disgraceful and embarassing", and an "indelible stain on the country of Norway". He has long indicated he thought he should have been awarded the prestigious prize, and was nominated by several allies for it last year.Related topicsInternational Criminal CourtDonald TrumpUnited StatesNobel PrizeHuman rightsMore on this storyUS unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'Published2 days ago'Stain on the country': Trump criticises Norway over Nobel Peace PrizePublished1 day ago

title: Riyadh airport attacks another dangerous moment in already tense conflict
content: Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, Houthi soldiers stand guard during a protest against Saudi Arabia, in Sana'a, Yemen, on FridayByFrank Gardner, BBC security correspondent and Jon Donnison, Reporting fromJerusalemPublished11 October 2026, 12:32 BSTUpdated 7 hours agoThe attacks on King Khalid Airport in Riyadh mark another dangerous moment in a region that is already fraught with tension and conflict.Saudi Arabia wasn't ready for this. In recent weeks the Houthis have stepped up their attacks on Saudi Arabian soil, but their attacks over the past few days have hit the country's critical infrastructure in the form of the capital's main airport, apparently penetrating Saudi air defences with ease.Saturday's attack killed 12 people and hurt more than 300. On Sunday the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said an "unknown projectile" had hit a passenger hall and a cruise missile had been intercepted nearby.The physical damage can be quickly repaired, but the country's reputation as a safe haven of stability is taking a battering.As well as all the airport attacks, the Houthis have sought to take control of strategically significant positions along the Red Sea coast and around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. This further increases the risk to safe navigation along the vital maritime corridor - although the Yemeni government says it has "secured" the strait.The civil war in Yemen between the country's government - which is internationally recognised and supported by Saudi Arabia - and the Houthis, who are backed by Iran, has been going on for more than a decade. It has left many thousands of people dead and plunged Yemen into one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.It is a complex and often confusing geopolitical conflict, and this latest escalation needs to be seen in the broader context of the tension between Iran, the United States and Israel.Who are the Houthis and what do they want?Published24 SeptemberHouthi attacks raise fears of wider Middle East conflict and more global economic damagePublished24 JulyChildren brave snipers and mortars to go to school near Yemen front line Published5 days agoNot since the al-Qaeda insurgency of the mid-2000s has the Kingdom faced such a serious threat. The Saudi government overcame that challenge through an effective hearts and minds campaign. Then it weathered the Arab Spring uprisings around the region which saw off leaders in Tunisia, Libya, Egypt and Yemen. It even shrugged off – with some annoyance – an Iranian ballistic missile attack on Riyadh in March.But this is different. Saudi Arabia may have one of the most powerful air forces in the Middle East, and it has been carrying out devastating air strikes on Houthi positions. Despite this, the opposing forces have managed to seize large portions of the country, particularly in the north and west.But the Houthis know exactly where to hit back: at the soft underbelly of the Saudi economy.As part of the "axis of resistance", the Houthis are a vital strategic partner for Iran. From Jizan on the Red Sea to the petrochemical complex at Khurais, the Houthis are delivering explosive drones and missiles with deadly accuracy.The Red Sea shipping route has become increasingly important, because the Strait of Hormuz, on the other side of the Gulf, has still not fully reopened since the US and Iran have failed to reach a deal to end their war.Targeting ships in the Red Sea is another way that the Houthis are trying to exert leverage - the attacks cause global economic damage, which is a key bargaining chip for Tehran.In early September, the White House stated it would not directly intervene in the Yemen conflict, but could provide intelligence support to the Saudis. It later confirmed that it was supplying intelligence and had deployed military experts to Saudi Arabia.However the situation may have taken a new turn following the latest attack on Riyadh, which killed a US citizen.Speaking to reporters, US President Donald Trump called Saturday's attack "terrible" and indicated he may intervene militarily with the Saudis. "We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," Trump said.But that now seems unlikely, at least before crucial US midterm elections next month.When he was re-elected in 2024, Trump promised to end America's role in wars around the world. Despite this, the US is currently involved in three unresolved conflicts in the Middle East - in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.Should Trump get embroiled in another one, this time in Yemen, it is unlikely to go down well with voters.This war now looks like it will intensify before it ends in another shaky truce - with or without US involvement.Additional analysis from Abdelbassir Hassan, BBC ArabicRelated topicsHouthis IranYemenSaudi ArabiaYemen crisisUnited StatesMore on this storySaudi Arabia's Riyadh airport hit by second Houthi strike in two daysPublished40 minutes agoInside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for controlPublished27 SeptemberYemen's government announces all-out war to reclaim land from HouthisPublished4 October

title: Blackpink’s Lisa Manobal: How the K-pop star faced a race scandal
content: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lisa, who was born Pranpriya Manobal in Thailand, became one of the world's most-recognisable K-pop idols as a member of BlackpinkByMark SavageMusic correspondentPublished11 October 2026, 00:31 BSTWhat's it like to be the main character of an online scandal?That's one of the questions raised in a new documentary about Lisa Manobal – one quarter of K-pop phenomenon Blackpink and a breakout star of TV show The White Lotus.The film captures an unfolding controversy, as leaked videos show Blackpink using racial slurs when they were teenage trainees in the K-pop system.The clips, which emerged last year, showed the band covering US rap songs during rehearsals. Explicit language, including the n-word, was left uncensored. The scandal blew up while Lisa was rehearsing for a pivotal performance at the Coachella Festival in 2025.Offended and upset, some fans demanded an apology - but the band's record label, forbade the members from issuing a statement.With Lisa's team in crisis mode, documentarian Sue Kim followed Lisa into her dressing room."I said, 'Look, I know this is new. I know you guys are wildly confused and hurt, but this is your time to say whatever you want to say - even if you're just processing your thoughts and telling us what you're feeling," Kim tells the BBC.The film-maker "honestly expected her to say no".Instead, Lisa lay down on a sofa and spoke from the heart."It's bad," the singer says in the documentary, with a mixture of shame and nerves.Lisa explains she was "15 or 16" when the videos were shot and "didn't know that [word] was sensitive because I'm from Thailand and my first language is not English".Having only heard the term in rap music, she was unaware of its offensive history."Now I would never ever do that because, now, I've got education," she says. "Now I know better."But I did wrong."It is a vulnerable and human response - and nothing like the scripted PR apology you might expect. (Lisa has since apologised publicly, external in an interview with Variety, although some people remained unconvinced, external).Kim says Lisa’s in-the-moment reaction is "one of the most important scenes" in her documentary, Always Lalisa, which hits cinemas on Monday, 12 October."There was no premeditation on Lisa's part, there was no media training," she adds."I asked her one question and she just talked for an hour, and everything came out, and it's all stream of consciousness."And what you see with Lisa in that moment is so genuine, it's impossible not to feel compassion for her."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Sue Kim (right) followed Lisa for a year, as she launched her solo career during a break in Blackpink's activitiesThe incident overshadowed what was supposed to be a triumphant launch for Lisa's debut solo album, Alter Ego.In the film, the singer receives death threats, but presses ahead with public appearances while safety concerns are "spinning in my head"."To a certain extent I have to take [criticism] and compromise," she says, exhausted, "but sometimes, it's too much".In a world of sanitised celebrity profiles, Kim's portrayal of upheaval and discomfort is unusual. She asks Lisa about bad reviews, and captures the star being scolded by her vocal coach for lack of effort.That said, the documentary was commissioned by the film division of the star's record label (which also made the recent, and much less revealing, Oasis documentary), so it is still ultimately a marketing product.Even the most abrasive moments are calibrated to present Lisa in a good light - but the director credits the star with ensuring the film was not a mere puff piece."You never know when you meet an artist how transparent they'll be. And I have to give all credit to Lisa because she allowed us almost total access," Kim says."And when I showed her the film, she never asked me to remove a single scene. That's exceptional."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lisa put aside scandal and online death threats to put on one of the standout performances of 2025's Coachella Music FestivalImage source, Sony Music VisionImage caption, The documentary captures Lisa's joy - and relief - after she pulled off the hour-long showThe film's main storyline is about Lisa taking a break from K-pop to pursue crossover success in the Western music market.When we meet her, she is one of the world's most famous women, with millions of record sales and brand deals with Louis Vuitton and Bvlgari.But she is trapped by a K-pop system that forbids her from drinking alcohol and having adult relationships."I don't want my dating to be the thing to hurt Blackpink's popularity," she says in the film. "But when I turned 25, I realised that this is not how you're supposed to live your life."As a result, Lisa makes an early decision to cut ties with Korean entertainment company YG, who discovered her as a teenager, and signs a new deal with RCA Records in the US."Knowing her as I do, that took an immense amount of courage," says Kim."In general, she is a very kind, sweet person - and sometimes personalities like that, they don't want to rock the boat."Having been trained in the K-pop system from an early age, she grew acclimatised to obedience. Declaring that she wants a break is such a disruption to that way of life that I can only imagine it must have been building inside her for years."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Blackpink are one of K-pop's biggest bands, with hits like Whistle, How You Like That and Kill This LoveThe potential rewards for going solo were phenomenal – but so were the risks.In the film, we see Lisa struggling to assert herself in the recording studio, and tearfully battling nerves over her singing voice.At the age of 25, she is still curiously child-like. The fierce independence of her solo single New Woman sounds more like aspiration than fact.Kim says that began to change as they filmed."I saw a person who was very tentative and unsure of herself slowly starting to unfold her wings. Making mistakes, but also getting back up on the horse."Kim locates an inner confidence in early home videos of Lisa competing in talent shows, drawing parallels between that precocious seven-year-old and the young woman who is gradually reclaiming her agency.She doggedly pursues a role in the third season of hit TV drama The White Lotus, self-taping an audition that wins her the role of kind-hearted wellness coach Mook Sornsin.On set, she shrugs off the restrictive moral code of her pop career."Lisa threw more parties than anyone else," notes the show's executive producer in an interview."And the defining characteristic of a Lisa party is tequila shots."Image source, Fabio Lovino / HBOImage caption, The singer made her acting debut in season three of The White Lotus, filmed on location in her home countryKim did not partake in the hedonism. In fact, the film-maker and her crew were regularly falling sick as they tried to keep up with Lisa's ridiculous schedule."But when we premiered the film in Toronto, Lisa found me and she brought bottles of tequila, and that was like the perfect christening of the film," she laughs.The movie ends in June 2025 as Lisa returns to Seoul and rejoins Blackpink. As she unpacks her bags, she is clearly conflicted."It's bittersweet, and I think that's OK," says Kim."I don't think people should take it as like, 'Oh, she hates Blackpink'. It's more that she was reflecting on this year of freedom and worrying that she wouldn't be able to retain that. And that's a very astute fear to have."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lisa won the award for best pop act at this year's MTV Awards, becoming the first K-pop star to lift the trophyIn the year since, Lisa has already wrapped up her Blackpink duties and started phase two of her solo career with the single Sawadika. Kim says she is not surprised."Spending the year away from the K-pop system in the US really opened her horizons," the director says."She was exposed to a different kind of entertainment system where they're not held to a vow of chastity. If two star performers link up, it's almost like they get more power."That gave her a sense of like, 'Oh, I could have a different life. I might not lose my career if I want to get married and have children'."So I think part of the reason why Lisa's interested in continuing her solo career is that it might give her a little bit more personal freedom to be who she is."Related topicsFilmK-popBLACKPINKMusicMore on this storyBlackpink: K-pop band make 'epic Wembley dream' come truePublished16 August 2025From Squid Game to Blackpink, how South Korea became a culture powerhousePublished28 December 2024Blackpink star Lisa joins White Lotus castPublished13 February 2024

title: Myanmar's young men live in fear of being snatched off the streets and sold to the army
content: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Authorities in Myanmar have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas, leading to corruption, extortion and abductionsByGavin Butler and BBC Burmese Published10 October 2026You do not stay out after dark if you're young and able-bodied in Hpa-An, the capital of Myanmar's southern Karen state. In recent months this has become conventional wisdom.But Zaw Min has no choice."I worry, but I have to go out to work," says the 26-year-old tuk tuk driver, who asked that his real name be omitted out of fear for his safety. "My family call me all the time and remind me not to drive passengers too far; to be careful who I take as a passenger... I have to be vigilant all the time."People are panicked and frightened," he explains. "Some people I know have been taken."Locals say plain-clothed members and supporters of the Myanmar junta have been roaming the streets of Hpa-An, arbitrarily arresting people in their teens, 20s and 30s and forcing them into military service.According to leaked documents seen by BBC Burmese, authorities have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas across jurisdictions, bolstering the junta's ranks as it endures a war of attrition against ethnic militias, pro-democracy groups and civilian-led resistance movements.Zaw Min is the only one among his siblings who is at the age of recruitment. Many other "kids" his age have fled, he says – to Thailand, or the homes of relatives further afield. Those who remain are often under strict instructions from their parents: be home before dusk.Myanmar has been locked in a bloody civil war since February 2021, when its own military launched a coup d'etat and ousted democratically elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi.Three years later, following a string of humiliating losses, plummeting morale and soaring rates of desertion, the junta enacted a mandatory conscription law that required all men aged 18 to 35 and women aged 18 to 27 to serve at least two years under military command. Those who refuse face up to five years in prison.The enactment of the law "represents one of the most severe and impactful actions taken against the entire civilian population since the military coup", according to Maj Naung Yoe, military affairs official at the Myanmar Defense and Security Institute (MDSI) and a former military officer who defected and joined the anti-coup Civil Disobedience Movement.Image source, Telegram/@pyithusittImage caption, An estimated 100,000 young recruits have been conscripted by the junta since early 2024Hpa-An is the latest to be caught in a dragnet that's already ensnared an estimated 100,000 young recruits over the past two-and-a-half years – many of them via coercion, extortion and abductions."Security forces track young people's movements to arrest them, force them into service under the pretext of statutory military eligibility, extort money through threats of detention, and arrest individuals during guest-list inspections," Naung Yoe says.The BBC contacted the Myanmar government's Central Body for Summoning People's Military Servants regarding incidents mentioned in this story, including the forced recruitment of conscripts and reports of abductions allegedly carried out in recent months.They said they had no comment on the matter.With the mandatory conscription law, the junta has established a human supply chain to sustain its armed forces. And it appears to have worked. Observers note that reinforcements have played a critical role in helping the regime claw back more territory. In many parts of Myanmar, the resistance is now on the back foot.The war, though, is far from over. And as more youths evade conscription – either to join the resistance or simply avoid armed conflict against their fellow countrymen – the junta's recruitment methods have become ever more extreme.International rights groups such as Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and Fortify Rights say Myanmar's military is abducting civilians and forcing them into military service.In July, open-source research organisation Myanmar Witness revealed that they had analysed hundreds of missing-person advertisements collected from Facebook between 2021 and 2025. Researchers found that missing person notices for January rose from four in 2021, pre-coup, to 82 in 2025, post-conscription law. "In practice, much of [the Myanmar military's] recruitment appears to be carried out through detention, coercion, and disappearance rather than formal call-up, and often without notice to families," they concluded.Men and boys constituted the majority of reported missing persons.Figure caption, Watch: BBC goes into jungle with Myanmar's civil war rebels"They are spreading rumours all over the neighbourhood that I sold my husband."Ma Moe San Pan sobs the words through gulps of air. She is sitting in her kitchen, at home in Yangon, where on the morning of 8 May 2025 she saw her 33-year-old husband Phyo Wai for the last time."We had an argument, and afterwards he left home," she recalls."I was upset and told my cousin about what had happened."Ma Moe San Pan's cousin worked at the local ward administration office, and she asked him to bring her husband back. It was two days later that Phyo Wai called her, from a military recruitment centre on the other side of the city.The cousin had taken him to the ward office which had sold him on to another ward for 4 million kyats ($900; £680) to fill that ward's recruitment quota, Ma Moe San Pan says. The BBC was unable to reach Ma Moe San Pan's cousin.In a desperate attempt to bring him back, Ma Moe San Pan was then scammed out of 4.5 million kyats by strangers who falsely promised his release.U Maung Maung Lwin, the administrator of the ward to which Phyo Wai was taken, later admitted to the BBC that he had played a role in sending him to the military recruitment authorities. When asked about allegations that individuals were being conscripted outside their home township, he said transfers from other townships do occur when local quotas cannot be met.But he denied that any money was involved in such cases, or in Phyo Wai's forced conscription."[Phyo Wai] told me they said they would help him and made him sign documents," Ma Moe San Pan recalls."If my husband had been legally selected for conscription through the normal process, I could have accepted that. What I cannot accept is that our own ward administration office allegedly sold him to another ward."I also regret placing my trust in my cousin."Image source, BBC BurmeseImage caption, Ma Moe San Pan says her husband was sold into military service by her own cousinIn the time since Phyo Wai was taken, Ma Moe San Pan has filed police complaints relating to two matters: the sale of her husband into military service, and the 4.5 million kyats she lost to scammers.The police accepted her complaint, she says, but refused her request to include human trafficking charges, claiming a human trafficking case could only be registered if a person had been sold abroad.She does not know where her husband is now.Ma Moe San Pan's case highlights a grim mutation of the junta's mandatory conscription laws: mounting pressure from the higher levels of the regime has created perverse incentives further down the chain of command.Surging demand and dwindling supply have fuelled an illicit market for eligible recruits. And with money on the table, security officials have taken to arresting youth at road checkpoints, tracking and ambushing workers during their daily commutes, setting traps via fake job advertisements, and forcibly entering people's homes, Naung Yoe says."Under the guise of the conscription law, these coercive arrests and recruitment drives have effectively transformed into a modern-day slavery and human trafficking enterprise."In late August, police in Yangon arrested a member of the Fire Services Department – a branch of the home affairs ministry – and his son-in-law for abducting four young men with the intention of selling them for military conscription.The reserve fire brigade unit commander allegedly deceived the men with promises of employment opportunities, luring them to his house and trapping them in a series of purpose-built detention rooms. Police officers raided the residence and arrested him on 25 August. He has since been charged with kidnapping or abducting in order to wrongfully confine a person, and faces up to 7 years in prison. BBC Burmese made several attempts to contact the police station where he is being held, but was unsuccessful."Lower-level administrative bodies, military personnel and local criminal gangs employ diverse tactics to press-gang and arrest young people," Naung Yoe says. "They sell these individuals to military units and regional commands facing manpower shortages, or traffic substitute recruits on behalf of wealthier individuals seeking to buy their way out of service."Image source, BBC BurmeseImage caption, It's been more than a year since Ma Moe San Pan last saw her husband Phyo WaiWhile conscription orders are indiscriminate on paper – demanding a quota of recruits from each village, ward, or township proportional to its population – wealthier conscripts can simply pay to dodge the draft and be replaced by someone more financially vulnerable.So it is the poor who disproportionately bear the burden.Naung Yoe, meanwhile, told the BBC that "these practices are escalating due to increasing difficulties in meeting monthly recruitment quotas and the lucrative financial profits made from recruit trading at the ground level".But the hardening fist of forced conscription also reveals the junta's empty hand, and its desperation for manpower.It "seems to be another step in the junta's efforts to enlist unwilling youth in a conflict that underscores its embattled position in the civil war" says Dr Sandeep Singh, a research fellow who teaches military studies at the National University of Singapore.The climate surrounding routine abductions, he adds, has "generated further difficulties on the youth of Myanmar, already affected by years of civil war, and their families".In addition to the daily anxiety of life in Myanmar, many would-be recruits now fear being forced to fight in a deadly conflict that they not only don't believe in, but actively oppose. This constant threat has fuelled massive internal displacement and severe labour shortages in an already flailing economy, and sent people fleeing to neighbouring countries.Having spent more than half a decade waging war against its own population, the junta is now wielding the conscription law as yet another tool of subjugation, observers say.As the MDSI put it in a statement published in June: "The generals have benefited by using military law to make the citizens fight against each other."Related topicsMyanmarAsiaMilitaryMore on this storyMillions opposed military rule in Myanmar. Is their dream of a revolution over?Published30 JulyFrom behind bars, Aung San Suu Kyi casts a long shadow over MyanmarPublished14 JanuarySoldier-spies in Myanmar help pro-democracy rebels make crucial gainsPublished20 December 2024The college scam that promised students fleeing war a new life in FinlandPublished12 June

title: Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago - why are they resuming now?
content: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, An estimated crowd of 20,000 gathered in Kentucky in 1936 for the public hanging of Rainey BetheaBySheila FlynnSenior US reporterPublished10 October 2026They came in their thousands from near and far. Men, women and children lined up on a Kentucky riverfront for the public hanging of a black man convicted of raping and killing an elderly white widow.It was 14 August 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky, a sweltering Friday in the middle of a legendary heatwave. Some slept overnight near the gallows to preserve their spots. Others held "necktie" parties the previous evening, arriving hungover as teenagers sold popcorn and soda to spectators.By the execution time of 05:00, the crowd had swelled to an estimated 20,000.That's when Rainey Bethea, an orphan in his 20s, stepped up to the gallows - sentenced to death after allegedly confessing to robbing, raping and killing Lischia Edwards, 70.The previous afternoon, he'd eaten a last meal of fried chicken, pork chops, mashed potatoes, pickled cucumbers, cornbread, lemon pie and ice cream.Many of those gathered - including press from as far away as Chicago and New York - came to see the rumoured "Lady Executioner". The local sheriff had died four months earlier and his widow had become his unlikely replacement. She declined to pull the trip lever herself, however, and it was a hired hangmen who instead sent Bethea to his death.That moment marked the last high-profile public hanging in the US. The circus surrounding Bethea's death embarrassed many in Kentucky and the governor outlawed public executions 18 months later.By then, most states had abolished capital punishment in view of the masses as societal attitudes sought more humane and private methods. Another hanging was attended by a few hundred in Missouri in 1937, but that was lesser known and marked America's final public execution - until now.Image source, FPG/Staff/GettyImage caption, Men, women and children attended the hanging, which marked the last high-profile public execution in the USA little more than 90 years after Bethea's killing, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the military would publicly execute Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 unarmed fellow soldiers in 2009 at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.The Pentagon followed up by saying the execution by firing squad in December would be livestreamed."People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.University of Colorado professor emeritus Michael Radelet, a long-time scholar of capital punishment, was shocked."I never imagined [another] public execution," he told the BBC.He noted how public support for the death penalty in general has been steadily declining - it was at 80% in 1994, for example, but now stands at 52%."It's gone down precipitously, especially when you give the alternative of life without parole," he said.It's too soon to know what the American public thinks of the idea of livestreaming an execution. But it's likely that millions or more will tune in.With Hegseth's announcement, Radelet said, "the justification for the death penalty becomes entertainment... bring your popcorn, invite your friends". Figure caption, Americans discuss their views on the death penalty after the botched execution in Tennessee of convicted murderer Christa PikeSonya Lea, who just last year published a book about Bethea's execution, "felt absolute horror for our descendants" when she heard of the announced firing squad livestream."What they called it in 1936 was a carnival of sadism," she said. "That we now have the technology that can make it go wider than the 20,000 people who showed up... to witness in Owensboro, Kentucky, it just makes it even more horrific."Lea's grandparents were teenage newlyweds among that 1936 crowd. She only found out after her grandmother's death in 2002, when she read an account her late grandma had given detailing how they were close enough to hear Bethea's neck snap.The author's subsequent years of research taught her that many Kentuckians were "haunted" by that execution."I really thought, with all my heart, that we had put this in the rearview mirror, this level of grotesquery that only a few countries in the world engage in - Iran, North Korea, Afghanistan," she said. "Are we now, as the United States of America, considering ourselves to be part of that kind of government? It's just horrific."But the polarisation and rhetoric in US politics may have set the stage for such an announcement, said Kurt Gray, a social psychology professor at Ohio State University."Some Americans might thirst for blood, but I think a lot of Americans don't and, if anything, I think a lot of other Americans are just kind of maybe desensitised," he said. "So it's not like they're cheering a public execution - they're just like, 'Oh, yeah, I guess that's where we're at now.'"Figure caption, Can the Fort Hood shooter’s execution be livestreamed?Other research indicates that Hegseth and the administration may be reading the country wrong.Garen Wintemute, director of the Violence Prevention Research Program at the University of California, Berkeley, said surveys point to a declining appetite for violence in the US."This morning, the chair of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops labelled this [livestream execution announcement] as barbaric," he said. "And I think he speaks for a lot of people.""I think it's this: a public execution is not who we are," he added. "It's not who we aspire to be as a country."The debate over Hegseth's surprise announcement appeared to be playing out within the White House on Friday. US Vice-President JD Vance expressed uncertainty to reporters about whether the public execution would go ahead as planned and said he would not watch it if it were livestreamed.Hours later, US President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan but that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.He did not answer the question of whether he'd watch Hasan's execution. "I really don't care how he goes as long as he goes," Trump said. "And I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."Related topicsUnited StatesKentuckyMore on this storyWho is Nidal Hasan? What to know about US plans to livestream an execution onlinePublished1 day agoFort Hood survivor supports gunman's execution by firing squad but questions livestreamPublished2 days agoI've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike'sPublished2 October

title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
content: Image source, Swedish Coast GuardImage caption, Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022BySarah RainsfordEastern and Southern Europe correspondentPublished10 October 2026Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children.Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks.But German police were already closing in on him.After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany.Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine".Both he and his country have denied any involvement.Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Police escort Serhii K to a helicopter following a hearing with the German Federal Public Prosecutor It was 02:03 on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea.There were two further explosions targeting both Nord Stream 2 – not yet in action, but already full – and the original Nord Stream 1 that had supplied around half of Germany's annual demand for natural gas.Both have been inoperable ever since.Prosecutors say "high-performance explosives" were planted approximately 80m (260ft) below the surface: four devices weighing up to 27kg each, activated with timers.They "strongly suspect" that Serhii K led a crew that included four deep-sea divers, using a rented yacht called Andromeda.Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat.As word of the blasts spread, experts and some governments initially rushed to the same conclusion: they blamed Moscow.Russia had a history of hybrid attacks, after all, and of using its energy supplies for political pressure.But as the airwaves filled with commentators citing "suspicious" Russian naval activity near the blast site, German police ignored the noise.They went on following the forensic crumbs.Eventually they led to Ukraine.The case since built by investigators alleges that Serhii K entered Germany for the Nord Stream attack on a forged passport, likely issued by Ukraine's security services.In the extradition files sent to Italy he is named as Serhii Kulinich.That might explain why he looked so calm on his holiday in Italy.He had been travelling widely, and without incident, for the past year. In a copy of his real passport seen by the BBC there are more than two dozen stamps from countries including France, Spain and Canada – all dated after the Nord Stream attacks.But by 13 August 2025, Germany had identified its key suspect and this time, when Serhii K crossed into Poland, he was detected.Italian police say the actual arrest warrant was only issued on 18 August after he had travelled south and left Poland, suggesting the Germans were not sure their neighbours would co-operate and detain him.By the time his wife made a booking at La Pescaccia though, he was officially a "wanted" man. As soon as he showed his passport at check-in at the resort, the local carabinieri got an automatic alert.Police arrived to make their arrest late that night, leading Serhii K away from the glamping site and his family in handcuffs.The saboteursNone of the Nord Stream suspects have spoken publicly and no-one admits any role in the explosions.But I have talked to some of the Ukrainians caught up in the case, and people close to them."Anyone who admits involvement in this mission, they're immediately a target for Russia," one source explained. "Whoever did it can never confirm that."Nord Stream was a major investment and worth big money to Moscow in fuel sales. But it also made Germany and others dependent, giving Russia immense leverage over Europe.That is why Ukraine, the US and Poland in particular all loathed it.Another source I spoke to was "eaten alive by anxiety" over the investigation and baffled that Germany, a close ally of Ukraine, was even pursuing prosecution."Many Ukrainians believe that these pipelines, they helped Russia to fight so blowing them up was a good thing for our country," they pointed out.The German prosecutor's office told me the justice system was outside of any politics.
