(Lisa has since apologised publicly, external in an interview with Variety, although some people remained unconvinced, external).Kim says Lisa’s in-the-moment reaction is "one of the most important scenes" in her documentary, Always Lalisa, which hits cinemas on Monday, 12 October."There was no premeditation on Lisa's part, there was no media training," she adds."I asked her one question and she just talked for an hour, and everything came out, and it's all stream of consciousness."And what you see with Lisa in that moment is so genuine, it's impossible not to feel compassion for her."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Sue Kim (right) followed Lisa for a year, as she launched her solo career during a break in Blackpink's activitiesThe incident overshadowed what was supposed to be a triumphant launch for Lisa's debut solo album, Alter Ego.In the film, the singer receives death threats, but presses ahead with public appearances while safety concerns are "spinning in my head"."To a certain extent I have to take [criticism] and compromise," she says, exhausted, "but sometimes, it's too much".In a world of sanitised celebrity profiles, Kim's portrayal of upheaval and discomfort is unusual. She asks Lisa about bad reviews, and captures the star being scolded by her vocal coach for lack of effort.That said, the documentary was commissioned by the film division of the star's record label (which also made the recent, and much less revealing, Oasis documentary), so it is still ultimately a marketing product.Even the most abrasive moments are calibrated to present Lisa in a good light - but the director credits the star with ensuring the film was not a mere puff piece."You never know when you meet an artist how transparent they'll be. And I have to give all credit to Lisa because she allowed us almost total access," Kim says."And when I showed her the film, she never asked me to remove a single scene. That's exceptional."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lisa put aside scandal and online death threats to put on one of the standout performances of 2025's Coachella Music FestivalImage source, Sony Music VisionImage caption, The documentary captures Lisa's joy - and relief - after she pulled off the hour-long showThe film's main storyline is about Lisa taking a break from K-pop to pursue crossover success in the Western music market.When we meet her, she is one of the world's most famous women, with millions of record sales and brand deals with Louis Vuitton and Bvlgari.But she is trapped by a K-pop system that forbids her from drinking alcohol and having adult relationships."I don't want my dating to be the thing to hurt Blackpink's popularity," she says in the film. "But when I turned 25, I realised that this is not how you're supposed to live your life."As a result, Lisa makes an early decision to cut ties with Korean entertainment company YG, who discovered her as a teenager, and signs a new deal with RCA Records in the US."Knowing her as I do, that took an immense amount of courage," says Kim."In general, she is a very kind, sweet person - and sometimes personalities like that, they don't want to rock the boat."Having been trained in the K-pop system from an early age, she grew acclimatised to obedience. Declaring that she wants a break is such a disruption to that way of life that I can only imagine it must have been building inside her for years."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Blackpink are one of K-pop's biggest bands, with hits like Whistle, How You Like That and Kill This LoveThe potential rewards for going solo were phenomenal – but so were the risks.In the film, we see Lisa struggling to assert herself in the recording studio, and tearfully battling nerves over her singing voice.At the age of 25, she is still curiously child-like. The fierce independence of her solo single New Woman sounds more like aspiration than fact.Kim says that began to change as they filmed."I saw a person who was very tentative and unsure of herself slowly starting to unfold her wings. Making mistakes, but also getting back up on the horse."Kim locates an inner confidence in early home videos of Lisa competing in talent shows, drawing parallels between that precocious seven-year-old and the young woman who is gradually reclaiming her agency.She doggedly pursues a role in the third season of hit TV drama The White Lotus, self-taping an audition that wins her the role of kind-hearted wellness coach Mook Sornsin.On set, she shrugs off the restrictive moral code of her pop career."Lisa threw more parties than anyone else," notes the show's executive producer in an interview."And the defining characteristic of a Lisa party is tequila shots."Image source, Fabio Lovino / HBOImage caption, The singer made her acting debut in season three of The White Lotus, filmed on location in her home countryKim did not partake in the hedonism. In fact, the film-maker and her crew were regularly falling sick as they tried to keep up with Lisa's ridiculous schedule."But when we premiered the film in Toronto, Lisa found me and she brought bottles of tequila, and that was like the perfect christening of the film," she laughs.The movie ends in June 2025 as Lisa returns to Seoul and rejoins Blackpink. As she unpacks her bags, she is clearly conflicted."It's bittersweet, and I think that's OK," says Kim."I don't think people should take it as like, 'Oh, she hates Blackpink'. It's more that she was reflecting on this year of freedom and worrying that she wouldn't be able to retain that. And that's a very astute fear to have."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lisa won the award for best pop act at this year's MTV Awards, becoming the first K-pop star to lift the trophyIn the year since, Lisa has already wrapped up her Blackpink duties and started phase two of her solo career with the single Sawadika. Kim says she is not surprised."Spending the year away from the K-pop system in the US really opened her horizons," the director says."She was exposed to a different kind of entertainment system where they're not held to a vow of chastity. If two star performers link up, it's almost like they get more power."That gave her a sense of like, 'Oh, I could have a different life. I might not lose my career if I want to get married and have children'."So I think part of the reason why Lisa's interested in continuing her solo career is that it might give her a little bit more personal freedom to be who she is."Related topicsFilmK-popBLACKPINKMusicMore on this storyBlackpink: K-pop band make 'epic Wembley dream' come truePublished16 August 2025From Squid Game to Blackpink, how South Korea became a culture powerhousePublished28 December 2024Blackpink star Lisa joins White Lotus castPublished13 February 2024

title: Myanmar's young men live in fear of being snatched off the streets and sold to the army
content: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Authorities in Myanmar have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas, leading to corruption, extortion and abductionsByGavin Butler and BBC Burmese Published10 October 2026You do not stay out after dark if you're young and able-bodied in Hpa-An, the capital of Myanmar's southern Karen state. In recent months this has become conventional wisdom.But Zaw Min has no choice."I worry, but I have to go out to work," says the 26-year-old tuk tuk driver, who asked that his real name be omitted out of fear for his safety. "My family call me all the time and remind me not to drive passengers too far; to be careful who I take as a passenger... I have to be vigilant all the time."People are panicked and frightened," he explains. "Some people I know have been taken."Locals say plain-clothed members and supporters of the Myanmar junta have been roaming the streets of Hpa-An, arbitrarily arresting people in their teens, 20s and 30s and forcing them into military service.According to leaked documents seen by BBC Burmese, authorities have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas across jurisdictions, bolstering the junta's ranks as it endures a war of attrition against ethnic militias, pro-democracy groups and civilian-led resistance movements.Zaw Min is the only one among his siblings who is at the age of recruitment. Many other "kids" his age have fled, he says – to Thailand, or the homes of relatives further afield. Those who remain are often under strict instructions from their parents: be home before dusk.Myanmar has been locked in a bloody civil war since February 2021, when its own military launched a coup d'etat and ousted democratically elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi.Three years later, following a string of humiliating losses, plummeting morale and soaring rates of desertion, the junta enacted a mandatory conscription law that required all men aged 18 to 35 and women aged 18 to 27 to serve at least two years under military command. Those who refuse face up to five years in prison.The enactment of the law "represents one of the most severe and impactful actions taken against the entire civilian population since the military coup", according to Maj Naung Yoe, military affairs official at the Myanmar Defense and Security Institute (MDSI) and a former military officer who defected and joined the anti-coup Civil Disobedience Movement.Image source, Telegram/@pyithusittImage caption, An estimated 100,000 young recruits have been conscripted by the junta since early 2024Hpa-An is the latest to be caught in a dragnet that's already ensnared an estimated 100,000 young recruits over the past two-and-a-half years – many of them via coercion, extortion and abductions."Security forces track young people's movements to arrest them, force them into service under the pretext of statutory military eligibility, extort money through threats of detention, and arrest individuals during guest-list inspections," Naung Yoe says.The BBC contacted the Myanmar government's Central Body for Summoning People's Military Servants regarding incidents mentioned in this story, including the forced recruitment of conscripts and reports of abductions allegedly carried out in recent months.They said they had no comment on the matter.With the mandatory conscription law, the junta has established a human supply chain to sustain its armed forces. And it appears to have worked. Observers note that reinforcements have played a critical role in helping the regime claw back more territory. In many parts of Myanmar, the resistance is now on the back foot.The war, though, is far from over. And as more youths evade conscription – either to join the resistance or simply avoid armed conflict against their fellow countrymen – the junta's recruitment methods have become ever more extreme.International rights groups such as Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and Fortify Rights say Myanmar's military is abducting civilians and forcing them into military service.In July, open-source research organisation Myanmar Witness revealed that they had analysed hundreds of missing-person advertisements collected from Facebook between 2021 and 2025. Researchers found that missing person notices for January rose from four in 2021, pre-coup, to 82 in 2025, post-conscription law. "In practice, much of [the Myanmar military's] recruitment appears to be carried out through detention, coercion, and disappearance rather than formal call-up, and often without notice to families," they concluded.Men and boys constituted the majority of reported missing persons.Figure caption, Watch: BBC goes into jungle with Myanmar's civil war rebels"They are spreading rumours all over the neighbourhood that I sold my husband."Ma Moe San Pan sobs the words through gulps of air. She is sitting in her kitchen, at home in Yangon, where on the morning of 8 May 2025 she saw her 33-year-old husband Phyo Wai for the last time."We had an argument, and afterwards he left home," she recalls."I was upset and told my cousin about what had happened."Ma Moe San Pan's cousin worked at the local ward administration office, and she asked him to bring her husband back. It was two days later that Phyo Wai called her, from a military recruitment centre on the other side of the city.The cousin had taken him to the ward office which had sold him on to another ward for 4 million kyats ($900; £680) to fill that ward's recruitment quota, Ma Moe San Pan says. The BBC was unable to reach Ma Moe San Pan's cousin.In a desperate attempt to bring him back, Ma Moe San Pan was then scammed out of 4.5 million kyats by strangers who falsely promised his release.U Maung Maung Lwin, the administrator of the ward to which Phyo Wai was taken, later admitted to the BBC that he had played a role in sending him to the military recruitment authorities. When asked about allegations that individuals were being conscripted outside their home township, he said transfers from other townships do occur when local quotas cannot be met.But he denied that any money was involved in such cases, or in Phyo Wai's forced conscription."[Phyo Wai] told me they said they would help him and made him sign documents," Ma Moe San Pan recalls."If my husband had been legally selected for conscription through the normal process, I could have accepted that. What I cannot accept is that our own ward administration office allegedly sold him to another ward."I also regret placing my trust in my cousin."Image source, BBC BurmeseImage caption, Ma Moe San Pan says her husband was sold into military service by her own cousinIn the time since Phyo Wai was taken, Ma Moe San Pan has filed police complaints relating to two matters: the sale of her husband into military service, and the 4.5 million kyats she lost to scammers.The police accepted her complaint, she says, but refused her request to include human trafficking charges, claiming a human trafficking case could only be registered if a person had been sold abroad.She does not know where her husband is now.Ma Moe San Pan's case highlights a grim mutation of the junta's mandatory conscription laws: mounting pressure from the higher levels of the regime has created perverse incentives further down the chain of command.Surging demand and dwindling supply have fuelled an illicit market for eligible recruits. And with money on the table, security officials have taken to arresting youth at road checkpoints, tracking and ambushing workers during their daily commutes, setting traps via fake job advertisements, and forcibly entering people's homes, Naung Yoe says."Under the guise of the conscription law, these coercive arrests and recruitment drives have effectively transformed into a modern-day slavery and human trafficking enterprise."In late August, police in Yangon arrested a member of the Fire Services Department – a branch of the home affairs ministry – and his son-in-law for abducting four young men with the intention of selling them for military conscription.The reserve fire brigade unit commander allegedly deceived the men with promises of employment opportunities, luring them to his house and trapping them in a series of purpose-built detention rooms. Police officers raided the residence and arrested him on 25 August. He has since been charged with kidnapping or abducting in order to wrongfully confine a person, and faces up to 7 years in prison. BBC Burmese made several attempts to contact the police station where he is being held, but was unsuccessful."Lower-level administrative bodies, military personnel and local criminal gangs employ diverse tactics to press-gang and arrest young people," Naung Yoe says. "They sell these individuals to military units and regional commands facing manpower shortages, or traffic substitute recruits on behalf of wealthier individuals seeking to buy their way out of service."Image source, BBC BurmeseImage caption, It's been more than a year since Ma Moe San Pan last saw her husband Phyo WaiWhile conscription orders are indiscriminate on paper – demanding a quota of recruits from each village, ward, or township proportional to its population – wealthier conscripts can simply pay to dodge the draft and be replaced by someone more financially vulnerable.So it is the poor who disproportionately bear the burden.Naung Yoe, meanwhile, told the BBC that "these practices are escalating due to increasing difficulties in meeting monthly recruitment quotas and the lucrative financial profits made from recruit trading at the ground level".But the hardening fist of forced conscription also reveals the junta's empty hand, and its desperation for manpower.It "seems to be another step in the junta's efforts to enlist unwilling youth in a conflict that underscores its embattled position in the civil war" says Dr Sandeep Singh, a research fellow who teaches military studies at the National University of Singapore.The climate surrounding routine abductions, he adds, has "generated further difficulties on the youth of Myanmar, already affected by years of civil war, and their families".In addition to the daily anxiety of life in Myanmar, many would-be recruits now fear being forced to fight in a deadly conflict that they not only don't believe in, but actively oppose. This constant threat has fuelled massive internal displacement and severe labour shortages in an already flailing economy, and sent people fleeing to neighbouring countries.Having spent more than half a decade waging war against its own population, the junta is now wielding the conscription law as yet another tool of subjugation, observers say.As the MDSI put it in a statement published in June: "The generals have benefited by using military law to make the citizens fight against each other."Related topicsMyanmarAsiaMilitaryMore on this storyMillions opposed military rule in Myanmar. Is their dream of a revolution over?Published30 JulyFrom behind bars, Aung San Suu Kyi casts a long shadow over MyanmarPublished14 JanuarySoldier-spies in Myanmar help pro-democracy rebels make crucial gainsPublished20 December 2024The college scam that promised students fleeing war a new life in FinlandPublished12 June

title: Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago - why are they resuming now?
content: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, An estimated crowd of 20,000 gathered in Kentucky in 1936 for the public hanging of Rainey BetheaBySheila FlynnSenior US reporterPublished10 October 2026They came in their thousands from near and far. Men, women and children lined up on a Kentucky riverfront for the public hanging of a black man convicted of raping and killing an elderly white widow.It was 14 August 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky, a sweltering Friday in the middle of a legendary heatwave. Some slept overnight near the gallows to preserve their spots. Others held "necktie" parties the previous evening, arriving hungover as teenagers sold popcorn and soda to spectators.By the execution time of 05:00, the crowd had swelled to an estimated 20,000.That's when Rainey Bethea, an orphan in his 20s, stepped up to the gallows - sentenced to death after allegedly confessing to robbing, raping and killing Lischia Edwards, 70.The previous afternoon, he'd eaten a last meal of fried chicken, pork chops, mashed potatoes, pickled cucumbers, cornbread, lemon pie and ice cream.Many of those gathered - including press from as far away as Chicago and New York - came to see the rumoured "Lady Executioner". The local sheriff had died four months earlier and his widow had become his unlikely replacement. She declined to pull the trip lever herself, however, and it was a hired hangmen who instead sent Bethea to his death.That moment marked the last high-profile public hanging in the US. The circus surrounding Bethea's death embarrassed many in Kentucky and the governor outlawed public executions 18 months later.By then, most states had abolished capital punishment in view of the masses as societal attitudes sought more humane and private methods. Another hanging was attended by a few hundred in Missouri in 1937, but that was lesser known and marked America's final public execution - until now.Image source, FPG/Staff/GettyImage caption, Men, women and children attended the hanging, which marked the last high-profile public execution in the USA little more than 90 years after Bethea's killing, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the military would publicly execute Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 unarmed fellow soldiers in 2009 at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.The Pentagon followed up by saying the execution by firing squad in December would be livestreamed."People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.University of Colorado professor emeritus Michael Radelet, a long-time scholar of capital punishment, was shocked."I never imagined [another] public execution," he told the BBC.He noted how public support for the death penalty in general has been steadily declining - it was at 80% in 1994, for example, but now stands at 52%."It's gone down precipitously, especially when you give the alternative of life without parole," he said.It's too soon to know what the American public thinks of the idea of livestreaming an execution. But it's likely that millions or more will tune in.With Hegseth's announcement, Radelet said, "the justification for the death penalty becomes entertainment... bring your popcorn, invite your friends". Figure caption, Americans discuss their views on the death penalty after the botched execution in Tennessee of convicted murderer Christa PikeSonya Lea, who just last year published a book about Bethea's execution, "felt absolute horror for our descendants" when she heard of the announced firing squad livestream."What they called it in 1936 was a carnival of sadism," she said. "That we now have the technology that can make it go wider than the 20,000 people who showed up... to witness in Owensboro, Kentucky, it just makes it even more horrific."Lea's grandparents were teenage newlyweds among that 1936 crowd. She only found out after her grandmother's death in 2002, when she read an account her late grandma had given detailing how they were close enough to hear Bethea's neck snap.The author's subsequent years of research taught her that many Kentuckians were "haunted" by that execution."I really thought, with all my heart, that we had put this in the rearview mirror, this level of grotesquery that only a few countries in the world engage in - Iran, North Korea, Afghanistan," she said. "Are we now, as the United States of America, considering ourselves to be part of that kind of government? It's just horrific."But the polarisation and rhetoric in US politics may have set the stage for such an announcement, said Kurt Gray, a social psychology professor at Ohio State University."Some Americans might thirst for blood, but I think a lot of Americans don't and, if anything, I think a lot of other Americans are just kind of maybe desensitised," he said. "So it's not like they're cheering a public execution - they're just like, 'Oh, yeah, I guess that's where we're at now.'"Figure caption, Can the Fort Hood shooter’s execution be livestreamed?Other research indicates that Hegseth and the administration may be reading the country wrong.Garen Wintemute, director of the Violence Prevention Research Program at the University of California, Berkeley, said surveys point to a declining appetite for violence in the US."This morning, the chair of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops labelled this [livestream execution announcement] as barbaric," he said. "And I think he speaks for a lot of people.""I think it's this: a public execution is not who we are," he added. "It's not who we aspire to be as a country."The debate over Hegseth's surprise announcement appeared to be playing out within the White House on Friday. US Vice-President JD Vance expressed uncertainty to reporters about whether the public execution would go ahead as planned and said he would not watch it if it were livestreamed.Hours later, US President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan but that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.He did not answer the question of whether he'd watch Hasan's execution. "I really don't care how he goes as long as he goes," Trump said. "And I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."Related topicsUnited StatesKentuckyMore on this storyWho is Nidal Hasan? What to know about US plans to livestream an execution onlinePublished1 day agoFort Hood survivor supports gunman's execution by firing squad but questions livestreamPublished2 days agoI've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike'sPublished2 October

title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
content: Image source, Swedish Coast GuardImage caption, Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022BySarah RainsfordEastern and Southern Europe correspondentPublished10 October 2026Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children.Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks.But German police were already closing in on him.After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany.Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine".Both he and his country have denied any involvement.Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Police escort Serhii K to a helicopter following a hearing with the German Federal Public Prosecutor It was 02:03 on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea.There were two further explosions targeting both Nord Stream 2 – not yet in action, but already full – and the original Nord Stream 1 that had supplied around half of Germany's annual demand for natural gas.Both have been inoperable ever since.Prosecutors say "high-performance explosives" were planted approximately 80m (260ft) below the surface: four devices weighing up to 27kg each, activated with timers.They "strongly suspect" that Serhii K led a crew that included four deep-sea divers, using a rented yacht called Andromeda.Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat.As word of the blasts spread, experts and some governments initially rushed to the same conclusion: they blamed Moscow.Russia had a history of hybrid attacks, after all, and of using its energy supplies for political pressure.But as the airwaves filled with commentators citing "suspicious" Russian naval activity near the blast site, German police ignored the noise.They went on following the forensic crumbs.Eventually they led to Ukraine.The case since built by investigators alleges that Serhii K entered Germany for the Nord Stream attack on a forged passport, likely issued by Ukraine's security services.In the extradition files sent to Italy he is named as Serhii Kulinich.That might explain why he looked so calm on his holiday in Italy.He had been travelling widely, and without incident, for the past year. In a copy of his real passport seen by the BBC there are more than two dozen stamps from countries including France, Spain and Canada – all dated after the Nord Stream attacks.But by 13 August 2025, Germany had identified its key suspect and this time, when Serhii K crossed into Poland, he was detected.Italian police say the actual arrest warrant was only issued on 18 August after he had travelled south and left Poland, suggesting the Germans were not sure their neighbours would co-operate and detain him.By the time his wife made a booking at La Pescaccia though, he was officially a "wanted" man. As soon as he showed his passport at check-in at the resort, the local carabinieri got an automatic alert.Police arrived to make their arrest late that night, leading Serhii K away from the glamping site and his family in handcuffs.The saboteursNone of the Nord Stream suspects have spoken publicly and no-one admits any role in the explosions.But I have talked to some of the Ukrainians caught up in the case, and people close to them."Anyone who admits involvement in this mission, they're immediately a target for Russia," one source explained. "Whoever did it can never confirm that."Nord Stream was a major investment and worth big money to Moscow in fuel sales. But it also made Germany and others dependent, giving Russia immense leverage over Europe.That is why Ukraine, the US and Poland in particular all loathed it.Another source I spoke to was "eaten alive by anxiety" over the investigation and baffled that Germany, a close ally of Ukraine, was even pursuing prosecution."Many Ukrainians believe that these pipelines, they helped Russia to fight so blowing them up was a good thing for our country," they pointed out.The German prosecutor's office told me the justice system was outside of any politics. Sabotage is an offence against Germany's constitution.Equally frustrating for the Ukrainians I met was their own government's silence."At the very minimum, he's a military man, so if there are any questions, they should be addressed to the state, not to him," a close contact of Serhii K complained.Ahead of his extradition to Germany, his lawyer here in Italy told me his client had felt "abandoned".Image source, Omar Marques/Getty ImagesImage caption, Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from CroatiaGermany has a whole list of suspects, but only one other name has been revealed so far.Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August.He was there as a consultant on a new thriller film about the Nord Stream blasts, though he denies any role in the real-life operation.Travelling was a risky move, when he knew Germany was pursuing him.Zhuravylov has lived in Warsaw with his family since just before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and has his own business there installing air conditioning.He is also a keen and competent deep-sea diver.But he is a civilian.Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him.In a dramatic twist, he ruled instead that a Ukrainian attack on Nord Stream, if that was what happened, would be a "just" act in a "bloody and genocidal war".As one source close to the case put it to me: "The Poles don't like Ukrainians, historically, but they hate Russians and Germans even more."Croatia is a different matter.Political ripplesThe implications of this case reach far beyond the courthouse in Hamburg.After a slow start, Germany is now Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid. The far-right AfD party, currently riding high in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream case to bolster its argument that support for Kyiv needs to stop.It is awkward, at the very least, for the governments in both Berlin and Kyiv.It also raises questions about what constitutes a legitimate military target: who can hit what, and where, outside an open war zone.When asked about the explosions, President Zelensky has previously insisted that Ukraine "definitely didn't do that".This week, a foreign ministry spokesman went further."I find it very unfortunate that this entire discussion has come to focus on who blew [the pipelines] up, rather than who built them," Heorhii Tykhyi told the BBC, forcefully.He argued that Nord Stream had "untied Russia's hands" to go to war, because it no longer needed to transit Ukraine for its gas to reach Europe. "Did we warn about this? We did," Tykhyi wanted to know. "Did anyone listen to us? No, no-one did."First in the dockSerhii K will shortly become the first suspect to face charges in this high profile trial.Zhuravlyov's case could be merged, in theory, at a later date, though that would be complicated.Those who know Serhii K call him a patriot.He signed up to defend Ukraine when Russia invaded even though he had several children and was exempt - and fought until December 2023.His military ID shows that he was still in active service when the pipelines were blown up, meaning someone in Ukraine's military command knew exactly where he was and what he was doing.They are not saying, though.And in court Serhii K himself will not say a word, either.His legal team will argue that he is not authorised to reveal details of any activities as a soldier and produce sworn statements from two of his military superiors to back that up.I am told one of them will be the man widely named as the mastermind of the entire Nord Stream plot.Related topicsUkraineGermanyWar in UkraineMore on the Nord Stream blastsUkrainian man arrested in Croatia over Nord Stream pipeline blastsPublished19 AugustSabotage behind Nord Stream gas leaks, says EUPublished28 September 2022A journey to the site of the Nord Stream explosionsPublished18 November 2022

title: Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?
content: Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?CloseUS President Donald Trump has said Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an immediate "energy ceasefire".Moscow is yet to comment on the announcement and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky told US media it was "news to me".Trump also recently announced a US deal to import Russian diesel, in an attempt to bring the fuel price down ahead of the midterm elections.The price of diesel in the US has been high since the start of the war with Iran and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz.The BBC's Joe Inwood examines Trump's announcement and what might mean for the president ahead of the midterm election.More on this story.SubsectionWorldPublished1 hour agoShareclose panelShare pageCopy linkAbout sharingRelated topicsDonald TrumpFollow Donald Trumpclose panelYou are now following Donald TrumpUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.Volodymyr ZelenskyFollow Volodymyr Zelenskyclose panelYou are now following Volodymyr ZelenskyUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.Vladimir PutinFollow Vladimir Putinclose panelYou are now following Vladimir PutinUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.War in UkraineFollow War in Ukraineclose panelYou are now following War in UkraineUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.Read description

title: Buildings swept away as flash floods hit central Nepal
content: Buildings swept away as flash floods hit central NepalBuildings swept away as flash floods hit central NepalCloseA flash flood has washed away houses, bridges and damaged a hydropower project along a river in central Nepal. The army said on Sunday that it had rescued 49 people from flood affected areas, but five are still missing, the district's top official confirmed. It is believed that the flood was caused by a landslide upstream of the Budhi Gandaki River in the Gorkha district. Four bridges and nearly two dozen houses have been swept away, as well as a camp at a hydropower project along the river. Nepal is still trying to recover from catastrophic floods and landslides that swept through its border towns with Tibet two months ago, wiping out thousands of houses, destroying critical energy infrastructure and leaving thousands dead and missing.More on this story.SubsectionAsiaPublished12 hours agoShareclose panelShare pageCopy linkAbout sharingRelated topicsNepalFollow Nepalclose panelYou are now following NepalUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.FloodsFollow Floodsclose panelYou are now following FloodsUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.Read description

title: Why have hundreds of 'cockroach' protesters been detained in Delhi
content: Why have hundreds of 'cockroach' protesters been detained in DelhiWhy have hundreds of 'cockroach' protesters been detained in DelhiCloseProtesters were heard slamming on bus windows following their detention during an anti-government demonstration called by The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) in Delhi. The CJP shared a video on social media showing its founder Abhijeet Dipke being detained with other leaders shortly after landing in the capital. The movement started in May after India's Chief Justice likened some unemployed young people to "cockroaches". Delhi police denied permission for the demonstration to take place, with tens of thousands of security personnel deployed and roads barricaded. But the CJP had insisted it would go ahead. BBC correspondent Azadeh Moshiri, on the ground in Delhi, explains what the latest protest is about.More on this story. title: Watch: 'Time for Ukraine to get a new president', says Trump
content: Watch: 'Time for Ukraine to get a new president', says TrumpWatch: 'Time for Ukraine to get a new president', says TrumpCloseUS President Donald Trump has called for new leadership in Ukraine, criticising President Volodymyr Zelensky for striking Russian oil refineries."It's time for Ukraine to get a new president" he told reporters. On Friday Trump announced a deal with Moscow to import Russian diesel, a deal Zelensky described as "a gift" to President Putin.Read more about the rising tensions between the US and Ukraine.SubsectionWorldPublished1 day agoShareclose panelShare pageCopy linkAbout sharingRelated topicsDonald TrumpFollow Donald Trumpclose panelYou are now following Donald TrumpUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.War in UkraineFollow War in Ukraineclose panelYou are now following War in UkraineUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.Volodymyr ZelenskyFollow Volodymyr Zelenskyclose panelYou are now following Volodymyr ZelenskyUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.United StatesFollow United Statesclose panelYou are now following United StatesUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.RussiaFollow Russiaclose panelYou are now following RussiaUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.UkraineFollow Ukraineclose panelYou are now following UkraineUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.Read description

title: Trump says Ukraine and Russia have agreed 'energy ceasefire'
content: Image source, Getty ImagesByTinshui YeungPublished11 October 2026Donald Trump has claimed that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire", with Kyiv saying it would support such a move but Moscow yet to comment.The US president insisted that it was "effective immediately" but provided no details.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky initially expressed surprise at the announcement, before saying Kyiv would support it if Moscow did. He also accused Russia of striking Ukrainian energy facilities after Trump's post.Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to curtailing revenue for Moscow's war machine - so Russia can fulfil a recently-struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.The diesel deal, temporarily undoing sanctions on Russian imports, is attracting growing criticism. Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin. European officials and some US politicians, including from Trump's Republican party, have said they do not support it.The deal is Trump's latest effort to lower domestic fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, having spent months grappling with the political consequences of the war with Iran which has pushed up global fuel prices, particularly those for diesel.That has soured Trump's standing with the American public, who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.Figure caption, Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?Zelensky said it was "news" to him that an energy truce was in effect in comments to news site Axios, before writing on social media that his officials "look forward to clear details of America's dialogue with Russia"."Ukraine is ready not to strike at Russian energy and we count on Russia's similar readiness and on the agreement of the president of the United States of America on this," he said.The BBC has asked the White House for further details.UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support.Zelensky later said Russia had hit a power plant in Kyiv with a drone, causing power cuts, followed by strikes on energy facilities in the north-eastern Kharkiv region."All of this happened after the president of the United States made his statement about an energy ceasefire," he said.For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure.Moscow said the installations it hits were legitimate targets because they supported Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".The attacks have disrupted energy supplies on both sides.Image source, Telegram/CrimeanwindImage caption, Huge plumes of smoke seen rising in the skies from the site where the Slavneft-Yanos oil refinery in Russia is located on 6 AugustEarlier on Sunday, UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC that the UK did not support it, while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas echoed Zelensky's criticism of it on Saturday.The deal has also attracted criticism from politicians of both main US parties.Seven senators, including three Democrats and four Republicans, have published a statement saying Trump's deal "runs directly counter" to a law that had explicitly banned Russian energy imports."Congress was clear: the US should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our Nato Allies," they said, urging the Trump administration to "reverse course".Republican Senator Thom Tillis, one of the seven, told NBC News that the deal "absolutely will" put American lives at risk.On Saturday Trump accused Zelensky of wanting to "make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries following the Ukrainian leader's criticism of the diesel deal.The US president suggested that it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president".Zelensky pledged to hold elections - despite them being suspended by the Ukrainian constitution during wartime - if Russia agreed to a 60-day total ceasefire.The Ukrainian president previously resisted calls from the US for fresh elections, pointing to complications with holding a vote in parts of the country that are active war zones or under Russian occupation.Trump, however, has repeatedly accused the Ukrainian leader of using the war to stay in power.Meanwhile, strikes and fighting on the ground continue in the four-year-long war.Six people were killed in attacks on two Ukrainian cities on Sunday, regional officials said.One person was killed in Russia's Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, while another man was killed in a drone attack in the Russian-occupied Donetsk region, officials said.Related topicsVolodymyr ZelenskyWar in UkraineMore on this story'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after
